title: Verilog and Digital Design: From Transistors to a Working CPU
subtitle: A hands-on beginner course on VLSI, CMOS logic, sequential circuits and Verilog, with labs that compile and simulate real Verilog on your device
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: This course takes you from a single transistor to a working 8-bit processor, in 14 chapters. It starts with the VLSI design flow, the Y-chart and the four design styles, then the MOS transistor as a switch, CMOS gates and duality, latches and flip-flops. Then it teaches Verilog step by step: modules and gate primitives, data types and operators, adders, multiplexers and decoders, behavioural modelling with always, if and case, registers, counters and shift registers, delays and timing, testbenches, finite state machines, parameters, generate and memories, and finally the road from RTL to silicon, ending in a capstone where you build a tiny CPU block by block and write a program for it. There are 40 numbered figures (waveforms, schematics and timing diagrams drawn from the same ideas you code), numbered tables, a recap, a memory trick, an expanded ELI5 and a concept map in every chapter. 12 interactive labs: two CMOS switch labs, and ten labs that compile and simulate Verilog fully offline using the Icarus Verilog engine from the VeriSim project, with a console, a waveform viewer and self-checking testbenches. Every level starts unsolved, tells you what to build, gives a hint, and ticks its goals when the simulation passes. Sources and credits: the outline of the first chapters follows the TutorialsPoint VLSI Design quick guide (text, figures and labs here are original). The simulator is VeriSim by senolgulgonul, which packages Icarus Verilog (GPL v2 or later) compiled to WebAssembly; the unmodified engine files are included in the labs under their GPL-2.0 licence.

chapters.title: What is VLSI? The big picture and the design flow

maps.title: VLSI

summary: VLSI means very large scale integration: putting millions or billions of transistors on one small piece of silicon. Nobody draws that many transistors by hand, so engineers describe a chip in a hardware description language and let tools do the rest.
This chapter shows the whole road from an idea to a chip: the design flow, the three ways to look at a design (the Y-chart), the divide-and-conquer hierarchy, and the four styles of building a chip.
Verilog, the language you will learn, sits in the middle of that road. Knowing where it fits makes everything later easier to understand.

glossary.def: Very large scale integration: chips with huge numbers of transistors, today often billions.
Hardware description language. Verilog and VHDL are the two big ones. You describe hardware, you do not run a program.
Register transfer level: describing a design as registers and the logic that moves data between them. The level Verilog is mostly written at.
The tool that turns RTL into a netlist of real gates and flip-flops.
A list of gates and the wires that join them.
A chip whose logic can be reprogrammed after it is made.
An application-specific integrated circuit: a chip made for one purpose, fixed forever once manufactured.
A pre-designed gate or flip-flop from a library, placed and wired automatically.

keyPoints: A VLSI chip has more transistors than anyone can draw: we describe it with an HDL and let tools build it.
The design flow: specification, architecture, RTL, simulation, synthesis, place and route, sign-off, fabrication.
The Y-chart has three views (behavioural, structural, physical) and five zoom levels from system down to circuit.
Hierarchy, or divide and conquer, is how big designs stay manageable.
Four design styles trade speed, cost and effort: FPGA, gate array, standard cell, full custom.

items: ELI5. Imagine building a huge LEGO city with a billion bricks. You would never place each brick by hand. You would write a plan: a district, then streets, then houses, then bricks, and a machine would follow the plan and build it.

Now the real words. A VLSI chip has a billion tiny switches called transistors. Engineers describe the chip in a language like Verilog, check the description by running it on a computer, and then special tools turn it into gates and finally into a layout for a factory. The steps are called the design flow. The big blocks are split into smaller ones, which is called hierarchy.
Try it. Put the eight steps of the design flow in order in the practice section.
If you remember one thing: you describe a chip in a language, test the description, and tools build it.
Think of a very large city. Nobody plans every brick. The mayor decides the districts, each district has neighbourhoods, each neighbourhood has streets, and builders use standard bricks.
A chip is the same: a few billion transistors, organised into layers of blocks, built from a small library of standard parts.
Chips are classed by how many parts they hold. Small-scale integration had a handful of gates, medium-scale a few dozen, large-scale a few thousand, and VLSI tens of thousands and up.
Modern processors reach billions of transistors, so the old names have stretched, but the idea stayed: integration grew and design had to change with it. (See Table 1.1 below.)

items: How do you design something so big? You follow a flow. First a specification says what the chip must do. An architecture splits it into blocks and buses. Then comes the step you will do in this course: writing RTL in Verilog.
You simulate it to see if it behaves. After that, tools take over: synthesis, placement and routing, timing sign-off, and finally the factory. (See Figure 1.1 below.) (See Table 1.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 1.1. The design flow from specification to silicon. The green loop of writing and simulating RTL is where a designer spends most of the time.

items: A useful way to organise all this is the Gajski-Kuhn Y-chart. A design can be seen in three ways. The behavioural view says what it does. The structural view says which parts it is made from.
The physical view says where those parts sit on silicon. Each of these views also comes at five zoom levels: system, algorithm, register transfer, logic and circuit. (See Figure 1.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 1.2. The Y-chart. Design is a walk inward and between the three axes: from behaviour, to structure, to geometry.

items: Verilog covers the behavioural and structural axes at the register-transfer and logic rings. You can write what a block does (behaviour) or how it is wired from smaller blocks (structure). The tools then supply the physical axis for you. That is the whole point of a hardware description language.

The other key idea is hierarchy, also called divide and conquer. A chip is split into big blocks. Each block is split into smaller ones, and so on, until you reach gates. You design and test each small block separately, then plug them together.
You will do exactly this in chapter 5 when a full adder is built from two half adders.
Finally, how will your design be built? There are four common styles. An FPGA has ready-made programmable tiles: you load a configuration and it becomes your circuit.

A gate array has fixed rows of transistors and only the top wiring is custom. Standard cells use a library of pre-drawn gates placed automatically. Full custom means a person draws every transistor. (See Figure 1.3 below.) (See Table 1.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 1.3. Four design styles compared. Moving right buys speed and density, and costs design effort and money.

items: Two languages dominate hardware description: Verilog and VHDL. Both are standards, both describe the same kind of hardware, and many companies use one or the other. Verilog looks like C and is shorter to write, which is why it is a good first language.
Almost everything you learn here carries over to VHDL and SystemVerilog.

In the next chapters we climb up from the bottom. First the transistor, then the gates made from it, then memory. Only then will we meet Verilog, so that every line you write has a picture of real hardware behind it.
That is the habit that separates hardware designers from people who just write code.

summary: Every digital chip is built from one tiny part: the MOS transistor. For logic design you only need one idea: it is a switch controlled by a voltage on its gate.
This chapter looks inside the transistor just enough to see why it works, then throws the detail away and keeps the switch model: nMOS closes when the gate is 1, pMOS closes when the gate is 0.
We also meet the three operating regions and the current equations, because they explain why bigger transistors are faster and why gates take time.

glossary.def: Metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor: a switch controlled by the electric field of its gate.
The control terminal, and the two terminals between which current flows.
The gate voltage above which the channel forms and the transistor turns on.
The thin conducting layer that forms under the gate when the transistor is on.
Two types: nMOS conducts on a high gate and pulls toward ground; pMOS conducts on a low gate and pulls toward the supply.
The channel width over its length. A wider, shorter channel carries more current.
The three operating regions of the transistor.

keyPoints: A MOS transistor has gate, source, drain and a body. The gate voltage controls whether current can flow.
nMOS is on when the gate is high; pMOS is on when the gate is low.
Three regions: cutoff (off), linear (like a resistor), saturation (like a current source).
Current grows with W/L and with the gate overdrive Vgs minus Vt.
For logic we use the switch model: nMOS passes a good 0, pMOS passes a good 1.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, What is VLSI? The big picture and the design flow:
• A VLSI chip has more transistors than anyone can draw: we describe it with an HDL and let tools build it.
• The design flow: specification, architecture, RTL, simulation, synthesis, place and route, sign-off, fabrication.
• The Y-chart has three views (behavioural, structural, physical) and five zoom levels from system down to circuit.
• Hierarchy, or divide and conquer, is how big designs stay manageable.
• Four design styles trade speed, cost and effort: FPGA, gate array, standard cell, full custom.
ELI5. Imagine a tap in the kitchen. The handle does not carry the water. It just opens or closes the way. A very tiny tap with an electric handle is a transistor.

Now the real words. A MOS transistor is a switch controlled by the voltage on its gate. The n-type closes when the gate is high, the p-type closes when the gate is low. Inside, a high gate voltage pulls electrons into a thin channel between the source and the drain, and current can flow. A wider channel lets more current through, and so does a higher gate voltage.
Try it. In the lab flip the gate and watch the lamp: first for the nMOS, then for the pMOS.
If you remember one thing: a transistor is a switch: n-type on for 1, p-type on for 0.

A water tap is a good picture. A tap has a handle, a pipe in and a pipe out. Turn the handle a little and nothing flows. Turn it past some point and water runs, faster as you turn more. A MOS transistor is a tap for electrons, and the handle is a voltage rather than a hand.

Physically, an nMOS transistor is built on a slab of p-type silicon, with two islands of n-type silicon called the source and the drain. Above the gap between them sits a thin insulating oxide, and on top of that the gate. The gate and the silicon beneath it act like a capacitor.
(See Figure 2.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 2.1. An nMOS transistor. Raising the gate voltage attracts electrons under the oxide and forms a channel that joins source and drain.

items: When the gate voltage Vgs is zero, the two n islands are separated by p silicon and no current flows: the switch is open. As Vgs rises, the gate pulls electrons into a thin layer under the oxide.
Above the threshold voltage Vt that layer becomes a continuous channel joining source and drain, and current can flow: the switch is closed.

The pMOS transistor is the mirror image. It uses n-type silicon with p-type islands, and holes carry the current. It turns on when its gate is lower than its source by more than the threshold. Together nMOS and pMOS are called complementary, and chips using both are CMOS. (See Table 2.1 below.)

lesson.title: Table 2.1. nMOS versus pMOS
head: Property
nMOS
pMOS
rows: relative speed for the same size
slower (about 2 to 3 times), so it is drawn wider

items: Now the details of how the current depends on voltage. There are three regions. Below the threshold, Vgs less than Vt, the transistor is in cutoff: off, with almost no current.

Above it, the behaviour depends on the drain-source voltage Vds. For small Vds the transistor is in the linear region and acts like a resistor. For larger Vds it saturates and acts like a constant current source. (See Figure 2.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 2.2. Drain current against drain-source voltage for four gate voltages. The dot on each curve marks the change from linear to saturation, where Vds = Vgs - Vt.

items: The simple long-channel model gives these formulas. In the linear region the current is k times (Vgs minus Vt) times Vds minus half of Vds squared. In saturation it is k over two times (Vgs minus Vt) squared.
The constant k is the transistor strength: the carrier mobility times the oxide capacitance per area times W over L. (See Table 2.2 below.)

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} I_D = k\left[(V_{GS}-V_t)\,V_{DS}-\tfrac12 V_{DS}^2\right]\ \ (V_{DS} < V_{GS}-V_t), \\[0.6em] I_D = \tfrac{k}{2}(V_{GS}-V_t)^2\ \ (V_{DS} \ge V_{GS}-V_t), \\[0.6em] k=\mu C_{ox}\frac{W}{L} \end{gathered}

rows: Vgs above Vt and Vds below Vgs - Vt

items: Why does this matter for logic design? Because it tells you what makes gates fast. A wider transistor (larger W) or a shorter one (smaller L) has a larger k, so it delivers more current and charges the next gate sooner. Higher supply voltage does too.
But bigger transistors also load the previous gate, so speed is always a trade. (See Table 2.3 below.)

head: Knob

rows: more area, more load on the driver

items: For designing logic you can now forget the equations. Use the switch model. An nMOS is a switch that closes when its gate is 1. A pMOS closes when its gate is 0.

One small caution: an nMOS passes a perfect 0 but a weakened 1 (it loses a threshold), and a pMOS passes a perfect 1 but a weakened 0. That is why logic gates use nMOS to pull down and pMOS to pull up. (See Figure 2.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 2.3. The switch model. This is the only picture of the transistor you need to design logic.

items: Try the first lab now. You will flip a gate voltage and see an nMOS and a pMOS open and close, and then connect the two to make an inverter. It is the shortest path from silicon to logic.
Memory trick: N is one, P is zero. nMOS conducts on one, pMOS on zero: 'N is oN for one, P is on for Plain zero.'

chapters.title: CMOS logic: the inverter, NAND, NOR and complex gates

maps.title: CMOS logic
links: Pull-up network | is the dual of | Pull-down network

summary: Put a pMOS on top and an nMOS on the bottom, tie their gates together, and you have an inverter. Add more transistors in series and parallel and you get NAND, NOR and any other gate.

The one rule to remember is duality: wherever the pull-down network has transistors in series, the pull-up network has them in parallel, and vice versa. One network is always on, the other off, so a CMOS gate wastes almost no power when it is not switching.
The lab lets you build the gates yourself by choosing series or parallel and checking the truth table.

glossary.def: Complementary MOS: logic built from pMOS pull-up and nMOS pull-down networks.
pMOS transistors connecting the output to the supply VDD.
nMOS transistors connecting the output to ground.
The pull-up is the pull-down with series and parallel swapped.
How much unwanted voltage a logic level can take before it is misread.
Power spent charging and discharging capacitances each time a signal switches: alpha C V squared f.
A single-stage gate that computes something like NOT (A AND B OR C).

keyPoints: CMOS inverter: pMOS to VDD, nMOS to ground, gates joined. Output is NOT input.
NAND: nMOS in series, pMOS in parallel. NOR: nMOS in parallel, pMOS in series.
The pull-up and pull-down networks are duals; exactly one conducts for any input.
Static CMOS draws almost no steady current; power is spent while switching (alpha C V squared f).
Complex gates compute AND-OR-INVERT functions in one stage.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, The transistor as a switch: the MOSFET:
• A MOS transistor has gate, source, drain and a body. The gate voltage controls whether current can flow.
• nMOS is on when the gate is high; pMOS is on when the gate is low.
• Three regions: cutoff (off), linear (like a resistor), saturation (like a current source).
• Current grows with W/L and with the gate overdrive Vgs minus Vt.
• For logic we use the switch model: nMOS passes a good 0, pMOS passes a good 1.

ELI5. Imagine a seesaw with a rope on each end. One rope pulls the board up to the roof, the other pulls it down to the floor. You are only ever pulling one rope at a time. Whichever you pull, the board goes all the way to one end.

Now the real words. A CMOS inverter has a p-type switch to the supply and an n-type switch to ground, both controlled by the input. Exactly one is on, so the output is pulled all the way up or all the way down, and it is always the opposite of the input.
NAND puts the n-type switches in a row and the p-type switches side by side. NOR does the opposite. The rule is duality: swap series and parallel between the two networks.
Try it. In the lab choose series or parallel for each network until the truth table is perfect and the checker says no short and no floating output.
If you remember one thing: the pull-up network is the pull-down network with series and parallel swapped.

The inverter is the smallest gate. Connect a pMOS between the supply VDD and the output, and an nMOS between the output and ground. Join both gates to the input A. If A is 0, the pMOS is on and the nMOS is off: the output is pulled up to 1.
If A is 1, it is the other way round and the output is pulled down to 0. (See Figure 3.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 3.1. The CMOS inverter. For either input exactly one transistor conducts.

items: Notice what never happens: both transistors on at the same time. So there is no steady path from supply to ground, and no steady current. A CMOS gate only draws current while its output is changing.
That is the reason CMOS took over from older technologies, and why a billion-transistor chip does not melt while idle.

If you slowly raise the input of an inverter from 0 to VDD, the output does not move at first, then swings quickly through the middle, then stays at 0. The curve is called the voltage transfer characteristic.
The steep middle is useful: it means a slightly noisy 1 or 0 is restored to a clean level by every gate it passes through. (See Figure 3.2 below.) (See Table 3.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 3.2. The inverter voltage transfer curve, computed from the long-channel model. Region C is the narrow band where both transistors conduct.

lesson.title: Table 3.1. Inverter regions as the input rises

items: Now the two-input gates. For a NAND gate the output must be 0 only when both inputs are 1. So put two nMOS in series in the pull-down: both must be on to make a path to ground. The pull-up is the dual: two pMOS in parallel, so if either input is 0 there is a path to VDD. (See Figure 3.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 3.3. NAND and NOR. Series nMOS make an AND of the inputs on the way to ground; the dual pMOS network does the rest.

items: NOR is the other way round. The output must be 1 only when both inputs are 0, so the two pMOS go in series in the pull-up. The pull-down is two nMOS in parallel: either input being 1 pulls the output to ground.
A quick check helps: NAND and NOR each have four transistors, and each input drives one pMOS and one nMOS. (See Table 3.2 below.)

items: Why are NAND and NOR the natural CMOS gates and not AND and OR? Because a single CMOS stage always inverts. An AND gate is a NAND followed by an inverter, so it is built from two stages and costs six transistors. A NAND is one stage with four.
NAND is also called universal: every logic function can be built from NAND gates alone, as the first Verilog lab shows.
The same recipe builds bigger gates in one stage. Take the function Y equals NOT of (A AND B, OR C). Its pull-down network has A and B in series, joined in parallel with C.

The pull-up is the dual: A and B in parallel, in series with C. This is called an AND-OR-INVERT gate, and it needs only six transistors where separate gates would need more. (See Figure 3.4 below.) (See Table 3.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 3.4. Duality for Y = NOT (A AND B OR C). Each series group in the pull-down becomes a parallel group in the pull-up.

items: A word about how these gates are drawn on silicon. Because one input drives one pMOS and one nMOS, layout designers line up the transistors so a single strip of polysilicon crosses both.

For complex gates they look for an Euler path: a route through the diffusion strips that visits every transistor once, so the gate can be laid out as one compact row. You do not need this to write Verilog, but it explains why standard cells look so regular.

The cost of using a gate is mostly the energy to charge and discharge the capacitance it drives each time it switches. This dynamic power is the activity factor alpha times the load capacitance C times the supply voltage squared times the clock frequency f.
Lowering the voltage helps a lot because it is squared; that is why chips run at around one volt. (See Table 3.4 below.)

chapters.title: Remembering: latches, flip-flops and the clock

summary: Gates alone have no memory: their output depends only on the inputs right now. To build counters, registers and processors we need circuits that remember.

The trick is feedback. Wire the output of a gate back to its own input and the circuit can hold a bit. That is a latch. Two latches back to back, with opposite enables, make a flip-flop that changes only at a clock edge.
Everything in a synchronous chip is built from flip-flops sharing a clock. The next chapters of Verilog describe exactly these parts.

glossary.def: Output depends only on the current inputs.
Output depends on the inputs and on stored state.
A level-sensitive memory element: transparent while enabled, holding otherwise.
An edge-triggered memory element: copies its input only at the clock edge.
A regular square wave that tells all flip-flops when to update.
A circuit with two stable states, which is what makes one bit of memory.
A half-decided state that can happen if data changes at the instant of the clock edge.

keyPoints: Memory comes from feedback: a bistable circuit with two stable states.
The SR latch (two cross-coupled NOR gates) sets, resets or holds. S = R = 1 is forbidden.
A D latch passes d while enabled and holds while not.
A flip-flop is two latches in series; it copies d only on the clock edge.
Flip-flop kinds: D, T, JK, SR. The D flip-flop is what Verilog registers become.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, CMOS logic: the inverter, NAND, NOR and complex gates:
• CMOS inverter: pMOS to VDD, nMOS to ground, gates joined. Output is NOT input.
• NAND: nMOS in series, pMOS in parallel. NOR: nMOS in parallel, pMOS in series.
• The pull-up and pull-down networks are duals; exactly one conducts for any input.
• Static CMOS draws almost no steady current; power is spent while switching (alpha C V squared f).
• Complex gates compute AND-OR-INVERT functions in one stage.
ELI5. Imagine a light switch in your room. You flip it on, you leave, and when you come back it is still on. The switch remembers. A normal wire cannot do that: when you stop pushing, it forgets.
Now the real words. Memory in a circuit comes from feedback: a gate whose output goes back to its own input can hold a state. Two NOR gates cross-connected make an SR latch with set, reset and hold.

A D latch follows its input while it is open and freezes when it closes. Two latches back to back make a flip-flop that copies its input only when the clock rises. A clock is a regular tick that tells every flip-flop when to update.
Try it. In the lab write the stimulus for the latch and the flip-flop and see on the waveform when q changes and when it does not.
If you remember one thing: a flip-flop copies d at the clock edge and holds it until the next edge.

A light switch remembers its state. Flip it on and it stays on until you flip it off. That is memory: the output depends on the history, not only on what your finger is doing right now. A circuit with memory is called sequential, because what it does depends on the sequence of events.

How can gates remember? Cross-couple two inverters in a ring. The first one's output feeds the second, whose output feeds the first. This ring has two stable states: left high and right low, or the opposite. Once it is in one of them, it stays there.
A circuit with two stable states is called bistable, and it holds exactly one bit.

To be useful we need a way to choose the state. Replace the inverters with NOR gates and use the spare input of each. S sets the output to 1 and R resets it to 0. With S and R both 0 the gates hold each other in place and the bit is remembered.
The one forbidden combination is S and R both 1: both outputs go to 0, and when released the result is unpredictable. (See Figure 4.1 below.) (See Table 4.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.1. The SR latch made from two NOR gates, with its truth table. The feedback loops are the memory.

items: The SR latch has two inputs with unusual meanings. A friendlier circuit is the D latch: it has a data input d and an enable. While enable is 1 the latch is transparent: q follows d. When enable falls, the latch freezes q at whatever d was.
You can build it from an SR latch plus two gates, so S and R can never both be 1.

A latch is sensitive to levels: while it is open, any change on d goes straight through. That is risky in a large circuit, because a signal can race through several latches in one open period. We want something that samples d at one instant only.
The answer is to put two latches in series with opposite enables. (See Figure 4.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.2. A master-slave D flip-flop. When the clock is low the master follows d and the slave holds. When the clock rises the master freezes and the slave opens.

items: When the clock is low, the master latch is open and follows d, while the slave is closed and holds the output. When the clock rises, the master closes, freezing the value d had at that instant, and the slave opens and copies the master to the output.
So q takes the value d had just before the rising edge, and holds it for the whole cycle. This is an edge-triggered flip-flop. (See Figure 4.3 below.) (See Table 4.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.3. Timing of a D flip-flop. Changes of d between the dashed rising edges are ignored.

items: Other flip-flop types exist and appear in textbooks. A T flip-flop toggles its output on every clock edge when t is 1, which makes a counter bit.

A JK flip-flop is an SR flip-flop that fixes the forbidden case: J and K both 1 toggles the output. You can make any of them from a D flip-flop plus a few gates, and in Verilog you simply write the behaviour you want. (See Table 4.3 below.)

Two other circuits are worth a name. A monostable circuit has one stable state and one temporary state: press a button and it makes a pulse of fixed length, then goes back. An astable circuit has no stable state and oscillates, which is how a clock is made.
A clock is the heartbeat of a synchronous design: a square wave, and every flip-flop updates on its rising edge.

Why do we build everything synchronously? Because it makes timing predictable. Between two clock edges the combinational logic has time to settle. At the next edge every flip-flop captures its input together.
As long as the logic is fast enough, you can reason about the circuit one clock cycle at a time, and Verilog lets you write it exactly that way.

The lab is a watching lab. The circuits are given and you write the stimulus: set and reset the latch, close the D latch, and change d around a flip-flop's clock edge. It is your first meeting with Verilog and with a waveform viewer, so do not worry about understanding every line yet.
The next chapter explains them.
Memory trick: A latch is a gate, a flop is a clock. Latch follows the Level; Flip-flop samples at the Flank: 'Latch = Level, Flop = Flank.'

quiz.q: What lets a circuit remember a bit?
options: feedback that gives two stable states
quiz.explain: A bistable loop.

quiz.q: In an SR latch made from NOR gates, which input combination is forbidden?
quiz.explain: It forces both outputs low and the result after release is unpredictable.

quiz.q: A flip-flop copies its input...
quiz.explain: It is edge triggered.

quiz.q: A master-slave flip-flop is made of...
quiz.explain: Master open on low, slave open on high.

quiz.q: A T flip-flop with t = 1...
quiz.explain: It divides the clock by two.

cards.a: Level sensitive, transparent while enabled.
Edge triggered: samples d at the rising edge.
Set, reset, hold; S = R = 1 is forbidden.
Toggles when t = 1.

cards.q: Memory trick for: Remembering: latches, flip-flops and the clock?

    $('#run').disabled = true; $('#status').textContent = 'compiling and simulating…';
    let r;
    try { r = await VL.run(files.map(function (f) { return { name: f.name, src: f.src }; }), L[cur].gen); } catch (e) { r = { ok: false, log: 'engine error: ' + e, vcd: null }; }
    last = r; $('#con').innerHTML = (r.ok ? '' : '<span class="err">') + esc(r.log.replace(/^VCD info:.*\n?/m, '').replace(/^\/[\w.]+:\d+: \$finish called at.*$/m, '').trim() || '(no output)') + (r.ok ? '' : '</span>');
    const res = evalGoals(r); goalsView(res);
    const all = res.every(Boolean);
    $('#status').textContent = r.ok ? (all ? 'Level complete.' : 'Compiled. Not all goals met yet.') : 'Compile error: fix it and run again.';
    if (all) { done[cur] = 1; }
    save(); chips(); drawWave(r.vcd);
    if (!completed && L.every(function (x, i) { return done[i]; })) { completed = true; try { if (window.lilith && window.lilith.complete) window.lilith.complete(); } catch (e) { } }
    $('#run').disabled = false; busy = false; return r;
  }
  function solve(i) {
    if (i !== cur) enter(i);
    const lv = L[cur];
    files.forEach(function (f) { if (lv.solution[f.name] != null) f.src = lv.solution[f.name]; });
    push(); return run();
  }
  /* ---- waveform ---- */
  function parseVCD(t) {
    const vars = {}, order = [], scope = []; let time = 0, end = 0; const lines = t.split('\n'); let defs = true;
    for (let ln of lines) {
      ln = ln.trim(); if (!ln) continue;
      if (defs) {
        if (ln.startsWith('$scope')) scope.push(ln.split(/\s+/)[2]);
        else if (ln.startsWith('$upscope')) scope.pop();
        else if (ln.startsWith('$var')) { const p = ln.split(/\s+/); const id = p[3]; if (!vars[id]) { vars[id] = { name: p[4], w: +p[2], depth: scope.length, ev: [] }; order.push(id); } }
        else if (ln.startsWith('$enddefinitions')) defs = false;
        continue;
      }
      const c = ln[0];
      if (c === '#') { time = +ln.slice(1); if (time > end) end = time; }
      else if (c === 'b' || c === 'B') { const p = ln.split(/\s+/); if (vars[p[1]]) vars[p[1]].ev.push([time, p[0].slice(1)]); }
      else if ('01xXzZ'.indexOf(c) >= 0) { const id = ln.slice(1); if (vars[id]) vars[id].ev.push([time, c]); }
    }
    return { vars: vars, order: order, end: end };
  }
  function valAt(v, t) { let r = 'x'; for (let k = 0; k < v.ev.length; k++) { if (v.ev[k][0] <= t) r = v.ev[k][1]; else break; } return r; }
  function hex(b) { if (/[xz]/i.test(b)) return b.toLowerCase().indexOf('x') >= 0 ? 'x' : 'z'; return parseInt(b, 2).toString(16); }
  function drawWave(vcd) {
    const cv = $('#cv'); const ctx = cv.getContext('2d');
    if (!vcd) { cv.width = 10; cv.height = 10; $('#wnote').style.display = ''; return; }
    const W = parseVCD(vcd); const ids = W.order.filter(function (id) { return W.vars[id].ev.length; }).slice(0, 16);
    if (!ids.length) { cv.width = 10; cv.height = 10; return; }
    $('#wnote').style.display = 'none';
    const rowH = 30, lab = 76, base = Math.max(300, $('#wave').clientWidth || 300), width = Math.floor((base - lab) * zoom) + lab, H = ids.length * rowH + 22;
    cv.width = width; cv.height = H; ctx.fillStyle = '#0a0712'; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, H);
    const end = W.end || 1, X = t => lab + (t / end) * (width - lab - 6);
    ctx.font = '11px ui-monospace,monospace'; ctx.textBaseline = 'middle';
    ctx.strokeStyle = '#2a2040'; ctx.fillStyle = '#7d72a0';
    const step = Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) * (end / 5 / Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) > 5 ? 5 : end / 5 / Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) > 2 ? 2 : 1);
    for (let t = 0; t <= end; t += step) { ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(X(t), 14); ctx.lineTo(X(t), H); ctx.stroke(); ctx.fillText(String(t), X(t) + 2, 7); }
    ids.forEach(function (id, r) {
      const v = W.vars[id], y0 = 22 + r * rowH, yh = y0 + 6, yl = y0 + rowH - 8;
      ctx.fillStyle = '#d6ccf0'; ctx.fillText(v.name.slice(0, 10), 4, y0 + rowH / 2);
      const evs = v.ev.slice(); const pts = evs.map(function (e) { return e[0]; });
      for (let k = 0; k < evs.length; k++) {
        const x1 = X(evs[k][0]), x2 = X(k + 1 < evs.length ? evs[k + 1][0] : end), val = evs[k][1];
        const bad = /[xz]/i.test(val);
        ctx.strokeStyle = bad ? '#ff7a9a' : '#7be0a4'; ctx.lineWidth = 1.5;
        if (v.w === 1) {
          const y = (val === '1') ? yh : (val === '0' ? yl : (yh + yl) / 2);
          ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1, y); ctx.lineTo(x2, y); ctx.stroke();
          if (k > 0) { const pv = evs[k - 1][1], py = (pv === '1') ? yh : (pv === '0' ? yl : (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1, py); ctx.lineTo(x1, y); ctx.stroke(); }
        } else {
          ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1 + 2, (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.lineTo(x1 + 5, yh); ctx.lineTo(x2 - 3, yh); ctx.lineTo(x2, (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.lineTo(x2 - 3, yl); ctx.lineTo(x1 + 5, yl); ctx.closePath(); ctx.stroke();
          if (x2 - x1 > 16) { ctx.fillStyle = bad ? '#ff7a9a' : '#ffd27f'; ctx.fillText(hex(val), x1 + 8, (yh + yl) / 2); }
        }
      }
    });
  }
  $('#run').onclick = function () { run(); };
  $('#hint').onclick = function () { $('#hintbox').textContent = 'Hint: ' + L[cur].hint; };
  $('#sol').onclick = function () { const lv = L[cur]; files.forEach(function (f) { if (lv.solution[f.name] != null) f.src = lv.solution[f.name]; }); push(); $('#hintbox').textContent = 'Solution loaded. Press Run to check it, and read it line by line.'; };
  $('#rst').onclick = function () { saved = {}; Object.keys(saved).forEach(function (k) { delete saved[k]; }); enter(cur); };
  $('#zin').onclick = function () { zoom = Math.min(16, zoom * 2); if (last) drawWave(last.vcd); };
  $('#zout').onclick = function () { zoom = Math.max(1, zoom / 2); if (last) drawWave(last.vcd); };
  $('#ed').addEventListener('keydown', function (e) { if (e.key === 'Tab') { e.preventDefault(); const t = e.target, s = t.selectionStart; t.value = t.value.slice(0, s) + '  ' + t.value.slice(t.selectionEnd); t.selectionStart = t.selectionEnd = s + 2; } });
  window.__lab = { lab: CFG, enter: enter, run: run, solve: solve, isDone: function (i) { return !!done[i]; }, setCode: function (n, s) { files.forEach(function (f) { if (f.name === n) { f.src = s; } }); push(); } };
  $('#rst').onclick = function () { Object.keys(saved).forEach(function (k) { if (k.indexOf(cur + ':') === 0) delete saved[k]; }); enter(cur); };
  enter(0);
})();
</script></body></html>

chapters.title: Your first Verilog: modules, ports and gates
summary: Now we can write hardware. A Verilog design is a collection of modules. A module is a box with ports, and inside it you describe either how it behaves or what it is wired from.
This chapter writes the smallest useful modules with the built-in gate primitives, connects modules together to build bigger ones, and shows what a testbench and a waveform are.
Remember the big idea: Verilog is not a program that runs step by step. It describes circuits, all of which exist and work at the same time.

glossary.def: The basic building block of Verilog: a named box with ports and contents.
A connection between a module and the outside: input, output or inout.
A named connection that carries a value between things; it cannot store.
A built-in gate such as and, or, not, nand, nor, xor, xnor, buf.
One copy of a module placed inside another; each has its own name.
A module with no ports that drives your design with inputs and watches its outputs.
Running the described circuit on a computer to see how it behaves over time.

keyPoints: A module has a name, ports (input, output) and contents. It ends with endmodule.
Gate primitives list the output first: and (y, a, b).
Modules are connected by instances: half_adder h1(.a(a), .b(b), .sum(s), .carry(c));
All statements describe hardware that exists at the same time; order of lines does not matter for wiring.
A testbench drives inputs and a simulator shows the waveform.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Remembering: latches, flip-flops and the clock:
• Memory comes from feedback: a bistable circuit with two stable states.
• The SR latch (two cross-coupled NOR gates) sets, resets or holds. S = R = 1 is forbidden.
• A D latch passes d while enabled and holds while not.
• A flip-flop is two latches in series; it copies d only on the clock edge.
• Flip-flop kinds: D, T, JK, SR. The D flip-flop is what Verilog registers become.

ELI5. Imagine you are writing a recipe card for a machine that builds a toy. The card says: take two blocks, join them in this way, and call the result a sum. The machine does not follow the card one line at a time. All the parts exist at once on the table.

Now the real words. A Verilog design is a set of modules. A module is a box with ports, and inside it you place gates or other modules and connect them with wires. Every statement describes hardware that exists all the time, not a step in a program. A testbench is a module with no ports that wiggles the inputs and lets a simulator show the waveform.
Try it. In the lab build an AND gate, then a half adder, then use two half adders to build a full adder, and watch every input combination pass.
If you remember one thing: Verilog describes hardware that all exists at once: modules, ports, wires.

In the last chapters we drew circuits. Writing Verilog means describing the same circuit in text. Here is a half adder: it adds two bits and produces a sum bit and a carry bit. In a schematic it is an XOR gate and an AND gate. In Verilog it is a module. (See Figure 5.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 5.1. A module is a box with ports. The text on the right describes the circuit on the left, line by line.

items: Read it like a recipe for a circuit. The first line gives the module a name and lists its ports, saying which are inputs and which are outputs. The two lines inside place two gates. Each gate primitive lists the output first, then the inputs.
So xor (sum, a, b) means: place an XOR gate whose output is the signal sum and whose inputs are a and b.

There is something important to notice. In a normal program, the second line runs after the first. In Verilog, both gates exist at once, like two physical chips on a board. If you swapped the two lines, the circuit would be exactly the same.
The text is a description, and there is no order of execution among the gates. (See Table 5.1 below.)

lesson.title: Table 5.1. The built-in gate primitives
head: Primitive
Meaning
Example
rows: odd parity, even parity of inputs

items: Signals that join gates inside a module are declared as wires. For example, a 2-to-1 multiplexer needs an inverted select and two AND outputs. You declare wire ns, t1, t2; and then use them to connect the gates.
A wire is just a named piece of copper: it carries a value from whoever drives it to whoever reads it, and cannot hold a value on its own. (See Table 5.2 below.)

lesson.title: Table 5.2. Port directions
head: Keyword
Direction
Inside the module you may
Typical use
rows: drive it and read it (with care)

items: Big designs are built by putting modules inside modules. This is called instantiation, and it is the structural style. A full adder adds three bits: a, b and a carry in.

It can be built from two half adders and an OR gate. The first half adder adds a and b. The second adds that sum to the carry in. A carry out happens if either half adder produced a carry. (See Figure 5.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 5.2. A full adder built from two half adders and an OR gate. This is hierarchy in practice.

items: Look at the instance lines. half_adder is the module being copied. h1 and h2 are the names of the two copies. Inside the brackets, each port of the half adder is connected by name: .a(s1) means the port called a is connected to the signal s1 in this module.
Connecting by name is safer than by position, because you cannot mix up the order by accident.

How do we know the design works? We simulate it with a testbench. A testbench is a module with no ports. Inside it you declare registers to drive the inputs, wires to watch the outputs, and an instance of your design.
An initial block then applies input values one after another, waiting between them.
Three new pieces appear. An initial block runs once at the start of the simulation. A hash followed by a number, like #10, means wait that many time units.

And the system tasks starting with a dollar sign are simulator commands: one writes the waveform file, one ends the simulation. The simulator turns the run into a waveform that shows each signal over time, which is how you see whether the circuit is right. (See Figure 5.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 5.3. The same multiplexer described at four levels. Gate level is what you used in this chapter; later chapters use the higher levels.

items: Verilog can describe a circuit at several levels of detail. Gate level, as here, places individual gates. The dataflow level writes the logic as an equation with assign. The behavioural level describes what the circuit does with if statements and loops.
There is even a switch level for single transistors. You will mostly work at the higher levels, but gate level helps you see what the tools produce. (See Table 5.3 below.)

lesson.title: Table 5.3. Levels of abstraction
head: Level
You write
Good for
rows: always blocks with if, case, loops

items: A few style tips from day one. Give modules and signals meaningful names. Use lowercase with underscores. Put one module per file in real projects. End every statement with a semicolon, except around the module header and endmodule. Comments start with two slashes. And always connect ports by name.
These habits save hours of debugging.
Memory trick: Output first. A gate primitive lists the Output first: and (OUT, in, in). 'Out first, then in.'

quiz.q: In and (y, a, b), which signal is the output?
quiz.explain: Gate primitives list the output first.

quiz.q: What do the two gates in a half adder compute?
options: xor for the sum, and for the carry
and for the sum, or for the carry
quiz.explain: Sum is a XOR b, carry is a AND b.

quiz.q: A wire in Verilog...
options: carries a value but cannot store one
quiz.explain: It is a named connection.

quiz.q: What is a testbench?
options: a module with no ports that drives and watches a design
quiz.explain: It exists only for simulation.

quiz.q: Does the order of gate statements in a module matter?
options: No, they all exist at the same time
quiz.explain: Verilog describes hardware, not a sequence of instructions.

window.__VLM = {};
const VL = (function () {

  async function inflate(b64) {
    const bin = atob(b64), u = new Uint8Array(bin.length);
    for (let i = 0; i < bin.length; i++) u[i] = bin.charCodeAt(i);
    const ds = new DecompressionStream('deflate-raw');
    const w = ds.writable.getWriter(); w.write(u); w.close();
    return new Uint8Array(await new Response(ds.readable).arrayBuffer());
  }
  const wasm = {}; let ready = null;
  function load() {
    if (ready) return ready;
    ready = (async () => {
      for (const n of ['ivlpp', 'ivl', 'vvp']) {
        const js = new TextDecoder().decode(await inflate(B[n + '_js']));
        wasm[n] = await inflate(B[n + '_wasm']);
        const s = document.createElement('script'); s.textContent = js; document.head.appendChild(s);
      }
    })();
    return ready;
  }
  const mod = (n, o) => window.__VLM[n](Object.assign({ wasmBinary: wasm[n] }, o));
  const CONF = g => 'basedir:/\nmodule:system.vpi\ngeneration:' + g + '\ngeneration:no-specify\nout:/out.vvp\niwidth:32\nwidthcap:65536\nfunctor:cprop\nfunctor:nodangle\nflag:DLL=vvp.tgt\n';
  /* files: [{name, src}]; returns {ok, log, vcd, err} */
  async function run(files, gen) {
    await load(); gen = gen || '2005';
    const code = [];
    const pp = await mod('ivlpp', { print: s => code.push(s), printErr: () => {} });
    const args = ['-L'];
    for (const f of files) { pp.FS.writeFile('/' + f.name, f.src.endsWith('\n') ? f.src : f.src + '\n'); args.push('/' + f.name); }
    pp.callMain(args);
    const err = [];
    const c = await mod('ivl', { print: () => {}, printErr: s => err.push(s) });
    c.FS.writeFile('/ivl.conf', CONF(gen)); c.FS.writeFile('/src.v', code.join('\n') + '\n');
    try { c.callMain(['-C/ivl.conf', '--', '/src.v']); } catch (e) {}
    let vvp = null; try { vvp = c.FS.readFile('/out.vvp'); } catch (e) {}
    const eText = err.filter(l => !/system\.vpi|dynamic linking not enabled/.test(l)).join('\n');
    if (!vvp) return { ok: false, log: eText || 'compile failed', vcd: null, err: eText };
    const out = [];
    const v = await mod('vvp', { print: s => out.push(s), printErr: s => out.push(s) });
    v.FS.writeFile('/sim.vvp', vvp);
    try { v.callMain(['/sim.vvp']); } catch (e) {}
    let vcd = null; try { vcd = v.FS.readFile('/dump.vcd', { encoding: 'utf8' }); } catch (e) {}
    return { ok: true, log: out.join('\n'), vcd: vcd, err: eText };
  }
  return { run, load };
})();

chapters.title: Data types, numbers and operators
summary: Real circuits carry many bits at once, so Verilog has vectors, number literals with a size and a base, and a rich set of operators. This chapter is the vocabulary of the language.
It also introduces the continuous assignment, assign, which says that a wire is always equal to an expression: the dataflow level of description.
Hardware signals have four possible values, not two. Knowing x and z saves you from the most confusing simulation surprises.

glossary.def: A connection driven by something else, for example an assign or a module output.
A variable that holds a value in procedural code. It becomes a flip-flop or just a wire, depending on how it is used.
A signal of several bits, written [msb:lsb], for example [7:0].
A written number such as 4'b1010: size, base, then digits.
Unknown, and high impedance (not driven). Two extra logic values besides 0 and 1.
A continuous assignment: the left side always follows the right side.
Gluing bits together with braces: {a, b}.

keyPoints: Signals have four values: 0, 1, x (unknown) and z (not driven).
A literal is size, apostrophe, base, digits: 8'hFF, 4'b1010, 12'd100.
Vectors are [msb:lsb]; use bit-select x[3], part-select x[7:4], concatenation {a,b}, replication {4{a}}.
assign y = expression; is a continuous assignment: hardware that is always connected.
Beware width: operands are extended to the widest size in an expression, which can change the result.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Your first Verilog: modules, ports and gates:
• A module has a name, ports (input, output) and contents. It ends with endmodule.
• Gate primitives list the output first: and (y, a, b).
• Modules are connected by instances: half_adder h1(.a(a), .b(b), .sum(s), .carry(c));
• All statements describe hardware that exists at the same time; order of lines does not matter for wiring.
• A testbench drives inputs and a simulator shows the waveform.

ELI5. Imagine a row of light bulbs that can show a number. Each bulb is on or off, and a row of eight is a byte. You can look at the left half, the right half, or the whole row. You can even swap the halves.

Now the real words. Verilog writes a many-bit signal as a vector, like [7:0]. You can pick one bit, a part of it, or glue pieces together with braces. A number is written with its size and base, like 4'b1010.
Signals have four values: 0, 1, x for unknown, and z for not being driven. The assign statement says a wire always equals an expression. The operators work on whole vectors at once.
Try it. In the lab swap the two halves of a byte with one line of concatenation.
If you remember one thing: vectors, sized numbers and operators let one line describe a lot of gates.

So far every signal had one bit. Real data has many: a byte has eight. Verilog writes a multi-bit signal as a vector. The declaration wire [7:0] x; means an 8-bit signal whose most significant bit is number 7 and whose least significant bit is number 0.
You pick out one bit with x[3] and several bits with x[7:4]. (See Figure 6.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 6.1. An 8-bit vector with its bit numbers, a part-select of each nibble, and a concatenation that swaps the two halves.

items: Numbers in Verilog carry a size and a base. The literal 4'b1010 means a 4-bit number written in binary. 8'hFF is an 8-bit number in hexadecimal, 12'd100 is a 12-bit decimal.

If you leave out the size, the number is at least 32 bits wide. Underscores are allowed to help reading: 16'b1010_0101_1111_0000. Always give a size to constants that go into hardware. (See Table 6.1 below.)

Now the types. A wire is a connection: it carries whatever is driving it. A reg is a variable that holds a value in procedural code, that is, inside always and initial blocks. The name is misleading. A reg is not always a register in the hardware.
It becomes a flip-flop only when the code makes it remember. We will see when in the next chapters. (See Table 6.2 below.)

lesson.title: Table 6.2. wire versus reg
head: wire
reg
rows: in code, yes; in hardware only if clocked
outputs of always blocks, testbench stimulus

items: Hardware signals are not always 0 or 1. Verilog has four values. 0 and 1 are the obvious ones. x means unknown: the simulator does not know, for example because a register was never reset. z means high impedance: nothing is driving the wire, as with a tri-state bus.
The values spread through logic, but not always: 0 AND x is still 0, while 1 AND x is x. (See Figure 6.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 6.2. The four logic values and an AND gate table. On the right, two drivers share a bus; a driver that is switched off outputs z.

items: When your simulation shows red x everywhere, it usually means a register that was never set, or two drivers fighting over one wire. Learn to love x: it is the simulator telling you something is uninitialised, which is better than silently giving a wrong 0.

A continuous assignment connects a wire to an expression: assign y = a & b;. It does not run once. It is a permanent connection, like a soldered wire with a gate. Whenever a or b changes, y is updated. You can write whole circuits as a list of assign statements.
This is the dataflow style, and it is shorter than gates. (See Table 6.3 below.)

Two pairs of operators are easy to confuse. Bitwise AND, &, works bit by bit on vectors and gives a vector. Logical AND, &&, treats each side as true or false and gives one bit. Similarly, == returns x if either side has x or z, while === compares them exactly and always gives 0 or 1.
Use === only in testbenches, never in hardware.

The reduction operators squeeze a whole vector into one bit by applying the operator across all its bits. &x is 1 only if every bit is 1. |x is 1 if any bit is 1. ^x is 1 if an odd number of bits are 1, which is the parity.
They are very short ways of writing a lot of gates, and you use them in the first lab level of this chapter.
The conditional operator is a multiplexer: assign y = s ? b : a; gives b when s is 1 and a when s is 0. Chains of them make bigger selectors.

The operators have a precedence order like arithmetic, with unary operators first, then multiplication, addition, shifts, comparisons, equality, bitwise AND, XOR, OR, logical AND, OR, and conditional last. When in doubt, use brackets.
Now the trap that catches everyone. In an expression Verilog first finds the widest operand, including the left side of an assignment, then extends every operand to that width before computing.

So assign {nb, diff} = a + ~b + 1; with a and b four bits wide is computed in five bits, and ~b is extended with ones on top before it is inverted. The result is wrong. The fix is to widen explicitly, as the chapter 7 lab shows. (See Table 6.4 below.)

lesson.title: Table 6.4. Common beginner mistakes with expressions
head: Mistake
What goes wrong
Fix
rows: a vector result where one bit was expected
forgetting the size on a literal
comparing with == when x is possible
result is x and an if takes the else branch
reset values so nothing is x
driving a wire from an always block

items: In the lab you write five small circuits with assign: a majority gate, a nibble swapper, parity and all-ones detectors, a maximum, and an adder with carry out. Each one is checked by a hidden testbench that tries many inputs. Remember to size your constants.
Memory trick: Bitwise and, logical and. One ampersand works bit by bit; two give one yes or no. 'One is Bits, Two is Truth.'

quiz.q: Which operator gives the parity of a vector?
quiz.explain: An odd number of ones gives 1.

quiz.q: Which value means a wire is not being driven?
quiz.explain: z is high impedance.

quiz.q: What is the difference between & and &&?
options: & is bitwise on vectors, && is a one-bit logical AND

options: y is always equal to a AND b
quiz.explain: A permanent connection.

  let zoom = 1;

  function chips() {

    $('#hintbox').textContent = ''; $('#con').textContent = 'Press Run.'; $('#status').textContent = ''; last = null;
    tabs(); push(); goalsView(null); chips(); drawWave(null);

  }

    last = r; $('#con').innerHTML = (r.ok ? '' : '<span class="err">') + esc(r.log.replace(/^VCD info:.*\n?/m, '').replace(/^\/[\w.]+:\d+: \$finish called at.*$/m, '').trim() || '(no output)') + (r.ok ? '' : '</span>');
    const res = evalGoals(r); goalsView(res);
    const all = res.every(Boolean);
    $('#status').textContent = r.ok ? (all ? 'Level complete.' : 'Compiled. Not all goals met yet.') : 'Compile error: fix it and run again.';
    if (all) { done[cur] = 1; }
    save(); chips(); drawWave(r.vcd);
    if (!completed && L.every(function (x, i) { return done[i]; })) { completed = true; try { if (window.lilith && window.lilith.complete) window.lilith.complete(); } catch (e) { } }
    $('#run').disabled = false; busy = false; return r;
  }
  function solve(i) {
    if (i !== cur) enter(i);
    const lv = L[cur];
    files.forEach(function (f) { if (lv.solution[f.name] != null) f.src = lv.solution[f.name]; });
    push(); return run();
  }
  /* ---- waveform ---- */
  function parseVCD(t) {
    const vars = {}, order = [], scope = []; let time = 0, end = 0; const lines = t.split('\n'); let defs = true;
    for (let ln of lines) {
      ln = ln.trim(); if (!ln) continue;
      if (defs) {
        if (ln.startsWith('$scope')) scope.push(ln.split(/\s+/)[2]);
        else if (ln.startsWith('$upscope')) scope.pop();
        else if (ln.startsWith('$var')) { const p = ln.split(/\s+/); const id = p[3]; if (!vars[id]) { vars[id] = { name: p[4], w: +p[2], depth: scope.length, ev: [] }; order.push(id); } }
        else if (ln.startsWith('$enddefinitions')) defs = false;
        continue;
      }
      const c = ln[0];
      if (c === '#') { time = +ln.slice(1); if (time > end) end = time; }
      else if (c === 'b' || c === 'B') { const p = ln.split(/\s+/); if (vars[p[1]]) vars[p[1]].ev.push([time, p[0].slice(1)]); }
      else if ('01xXzZ'.indexOf(c) >= 0) { const id = ln.slice(1); if (vars[id]) vars[id].ev.push([time, c]); }
    }
    return { vars: vars, order: order, end: end };
  }
  function valAt(v, t) { let r = 'x'; for (let k = 0; k < v.ev.length; k++) { if (v.ev[k][0] <= t) r = v.ev[k][1]; else break; } return r; }
  function hex(b) { if (/[xz]/i.test(b)) return b.toLowerCase().indexOf('x') >= 0 ? 'x' : 'z'; return parseInt(b, 2).toString(16); }
  function drawWave(vcd) {
    const cv = $('#cv'); const ctx = cv.getContext('2d');
    if (!vcd) { cv.width = 10; cv.height = 10; $('#wnote').style.display = ''; return; }
    const W = parseVCD(vcd); const ids = W.order.filter(function (id) { return W.vars[id].ev.length; }).slice(0, 16);
    if (!ids.length) { cv.width = 10; cv.height = 10; return; }
    $('#wnote').style.display = 'none';
    const rowH = 30, lab = 76, base = Math.max(300, $('#wave').clientWidth || 300), width = Math.floor((base - lab) * zoom) + lab, H = ids.length * rowH + 22;
    cv.width = width; cv.height = H; ctx.fillStyle = '#0a0712'; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, H);
    const end = W.end || 1, X = t => lab + (t / end) * (width - lab - 6);
    ctx.font = '11px ui-monospace,monospace'; ctx.textBaseline = 'middle';
    ctx.strokeStyle = '#2a2040'; ctx.fillStyle = '#7d72a0';
    const step = Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) * (end / 5 / Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) > 5 ? 5 : end / 5 / Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) > 2 ? 2 : 1);
    for (let t = 0; t <= end; t += step) { ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(X(t), 14); ctx.lineTo(X(t), H); ctx.stroke(); ctx.fillText(String(t), X(t) + 2, 7); }
    ids.forEach(function (id, r) {
      const v = W.vars[id], y0 = 22 + r * rowH, yh = y0 + 6, yl = y0 + rowH - 8;
      ctx.fillStyle = '#d6ccf0'; ctx.fillText(v.name.slice(0, 10), 4, y0 + rowH / 2);
      const evs = v.ev.slice(); const pts = evs.map(function (e) { return e[0]; });
      for (let k = 0; k < evs.length; k++) {
        const x1 = X(evs[k][0]), x2 = X(k + 1 < evs.length ? evs[k + 1][0] : end), val = evs[k][1];
        const bad = /[xz]/i.test(val);
        ctx.strokeStyle = bad ? '#ff7a9a' : '#7be0a4'; ctx.lineWidth = 1.5;
        if (v.w === 1) {
          const y = (val === '1') ? yh : (val === '0' ? yl : (yh + yl) / 2);
          ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1, y); ctx.lineTo(x2, y); ctx.stroke();
          if (k > 0) { const pv = evs[k - 1][1], py = (pv === '1') ? yh : (pv === '0' ? yl : (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1, py); ctx.lineTo(x1, y); ctx.stroke(); }
        } else {
          ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1 + 2, (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.lineTo(x1 + 5, yh); ctx.lineTo(x2 - 3, yh); ctx.lineTo(x2, (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.lineTo(x2 - 3, yl); ctx.lineTo(x1 + 5, yl); ctx.closePath(); ctx.stroke();
          if (x2 - x1 > 16) { ctx.fillStyle = bad ? '#ff7a9a' : '#ffd27f'; ctx.fillText(hex(val), x1 + 8, (yh + yl) / 2); }
        }
      }
    });
  }
  $('#run').onclick = function () { run(); };
  $('#hint').onclick = function () { $('#hintbox').textContent = 'Hint: ' + L[cur].hint; };
  $('#sol').onclick = function () { const lv = L[cur]; files.forEach(function (f) { if (lv.solution[f.name] != null) f.src = lv.solution[f.name]; }); push(); $('#hintbox').textContent = 'Solution loaded. Press Run to check it, and read it line by line.'; };
  $('#rst').onclick = function () { saved = {}; Object.keys(saved).forEach(function (k) { delete saved[k]; }); enter(cur); };
  $('#zin').onclick = function () { zoom = Math.min(16, zoom * 2); if (last) drawWave(last.vcd); };
  $('#zout').onclick = function () { zoom = Math.max(1, zoom / 2); if (last) drawWave(last.vcd); };
  $('#ed').addEventListener('keydown', function (e) { if (e.key === 'Tab') { e.preventDefault(); const t = e.target, s = t.selectionStart; t.value = t.value.slice(0, s) + '  ' + t.value.slice(t.selectionEnd); t.selectionStart = t.selectionEnd = s + 2; } });
  window.__lab = { lab: CFG, enter: enter, run: run, solve: solve, isDone: function (i) { return !!done[i]; }, setCode: function (n, s) { files.forEach(function (f) { if (f.name === n) { f.src = s; } }); push(); } };
  $('#rst').onclick = function () { Object.keys(saved).forEach(function (k) { if (k.indexOf(cur + ':') === 0) delete saved[k]; }); enter(cur); };
  enter(0);
})();

chapters.title: Combinational building blocks: adders, multiplexers, decoders

maps.title: Combinational blocks
links: Ripple carry | limited by | Carry delay

summary: With operators and assign you can now describe the parts every datapath is made of: adders and subtractors, multiplexers and decoders, encoders and parity circuits.
These are combinational: the outputs depend only on the current inputs, with no memory and no clock. Change an input and the output follows after a short delay.
The chapter also introduces a speed problem, the ripple carry, and explains subtraction through two's complement.

glossary.def: Adds two bits / three bits (two plus a carry in), producing a sum bit and a carry out.
A chain of full adders where each carry feeds the next.
The way computers write negative numbers so that subtraction is addition.
Selects one of several inputs under the control of a select signal.
Turns an n-bit number into one active line out of 2^n.
Reports the number of the highest active input line.
Whether the number of ones in a word is odd or even.

keyPoints: Combinational circuits have no memory: outputs depend only on inputs.
Full adder: sum = a XOR b XOR cin; cout = majority(a, b, cin).
Subtraction: a - b = a + (not b) + 1 in two's complement.
Mux selects, decoder one-hot decodes, priority encoder reports the highest set line.
A ripple-carry adder's delay grows with its length because the carry must pass through every stage.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Data types, numbers and operators:
• Signals have four values: 0, 1, x (unknown) and z (not driven).
• A literal is size, apostrophe, base, digits: 8'hFF, 4'b1010, 12'd100.
• Vectors are [msb:lsb]; use bit-select x[3], part-select x[7:4], concatenation {a,b}, replication {4{a}}.
• assign y = expression; is a continuous assignment: hardware that is always connected.
• Beware width: operands are extended to the widest size in an expression, which can change the result.

ELI5. Imagine adding numbers on paper. You add the right column, write the carry above the next column, and so on. Each column waits for the carry from the one before it. A row of little adders passing a carry is a ripple-carry adder.
Now the real words. A full adder adds three bits and gives a sum and a carry. Chain them and you can add numbers of any size, but the last carry has to wait for all the others.

To subtract, you add the two's complement: flip every bit and add one. A multiplexer chooses one of several inputs, a decoder lights one line for each number, and a priority encoder tells you the highest line that is on.
Try it. In the lab build a 4-bit adder from full adders and then a subtractor from one adder.
If you remember one thing: every block is a few lines of assign, and subtraction is addition with inverted bits plus one.

Adding is the most basic thing a computer does, so we start there. To add two single bits there are two results: a sum bit and a carry. This is the half adder, with sum equal a XOR b and carry equal a AND b. It cannot take a carry in, so it cannot be chained. For that we need the full adder.
(See Table 7.1 below.)

lesson.title: Table 7.1. Truth table of a full adder
head: a
b
cin
sum
cout

items: A full adder adds three bits. The sum is 1 when an odd number of the three are 1, which is a XOR b XOR cin. The carry out is 1 when at least two of the three are 1: the majority.

In Verilog this is two assign lines, as you will see in the lab. To add whole numbers, line up as many full adders as there are bits, and connect each carry out to the next carry in. (See Figure 7.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 7.1. A 4-bit ripple-carry adder. The carry travels from the least significant bit to the most significant one.

items: This is a ripple-carry adder. It is cheap and simple, but slow, because the top bit must wait for the carry to ripple through every stage below it. A 32-bit ripple adder is eight times slower than a 4-bit one.

Faster adders compute carries in advance with a lookahead network. Synthesis tools do this for you when you write plus, which is a good reason to prefer a + b over wiring full adders by hand in real designs.

That one line does the whole job. The left side is a 5-bit concatenation of the carry out and the 4-bit sum. The right side adds the operands and carry in. Because the left side is five bits wide, the addition is carried out in five bits, and the extra bit lands in cout.

How do computers handle negative numbers? Two's complement. In a 4-bit system, the patterns from 1000 to 1111 are read as minus 8 to minus 1, and 0000 to 0111 as 0 to 7. Picture the 16 patterns on a wheel.
Adding 1 moves one step clockwise; adding 15 is the same as going one step back, so 15 acts like minus 1. (See Figure 7.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 7.2. The sixteen 4-bit patterns on a wheel. The same bits read as 0 to 15 (unsigned) or minus 8 to 7 (signed).

items: This makes subtraction easy. To compute a minus b, add a to the two's complement of b. The two's complement of b is the bitwise inverse of b plus one. So a - b equals a + (~b) + 1, and the same adder does both jobs.
The carry out then tells you about borrowing: if there was no borrow the carry out is 1. (See Table 7.2 below.)

A multiplexer selects one of several inputs. A 2-to-1 mux has two data inputs and one select bit. A 4-to-1 mux has four data inputs and a 2-bit select. In Verilog the conditional operator is a natural way to write one.

Muxes are everywhere: they pick an ALU result, choose which register to read, or route data. A decoder is the opposite idea: it takes an n-bit number and raises exactly one of 2^n lines. (See Figure 7.3 below.) (See Table 7.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 7.3. A 4-to-1 multiplexer and a 3-to-8 decoder with an enable input.

lesson.title: Table 7.3. Selecting and decoding blocks
head: Block
Inputs
Outputs
One-line Verilog idea
rows: number of the highest set line, valid
nested conditional from the top bit down
1 if an odd number of ones

items: An encoder does the reverse of a decoder: it takes many lines and produces a number. A plain encoder assumes only one line is active. A priority encoder is more useful: if several lines are active it reports the highest one.
A valid output tells you whether any line was active at all, otherwise a zero number would be ambiguous.

A last combinational circuit is the parity checker. A word of eight bits is sent with an extra bit chosen so the total number of ones is even. At the receiver, one reduction XOR tells you whether the count is still even. If it is odd, a bit was flipped in transit.
It detects any single error, which is why parity is used on memories and serial links.

Notice the pattern in this whole chapter: every block is a few lines of assign. If you find yourself writing a long chain of gates, look for the operator that does it in one line. Let the tools find the best gates, and spend your effort on the design.

The lab has six levels: a ripple adder built from full adders, a subtractor, a 4-to-1 mux, a 3-to-8 decoder, a priority encoder and a parity checker. The subtractor level contains the width trap from chapter 6, so read the hint if the testbench disagrees with you.
Memory trick: Invert and add one. Subtract by 'Invert and add one': a - b = a + ~b + 1.

quiz.q: The carry out of a full adder is 1 when...
options: at least two of a, b, cin are 1
quiz.explain: It is the majority function.

quiz.q: In two's complement, a - b equals...
quiz.explain: Invert and add one, then use the adder.

quiz.q: Why is a ripple-carry adder slow?
options: The carry passes through every stage in turn
quiz.explain: Delay grows with the number of bits.

quiz.q: A 3-to-8 decoder with en = 0 outputs...
quiz.explain: No line is selected when it is disabled.

quiz.q: What does the valid output of a priority encoder say?
quiz.explain: Without it a zero code is ambiguous.

a - b = a + ~b + 1

grows linearly with the number of bits

    return new Uint8Array(await new Response(ds.readable).arrayBuffer());

  const wasm = {}; let ready = null;
  function load() {
    if (ready) return ready;
    ready = (async () => {
      for (const n of ['ivlpp', 'ivl', 'vvp']) {
        const js = new TextDecoder().decode(await inflate(B[n + '_js']));
        wasm[n] = await inflate(B[n + '_wasm']);
        const s = document.createElement('script'); s.textContent = js; document.head.appendChild(s);
      }
    })();

  }

  /* files: [{name, src}]; returns {ok, log, vcd, err} */
  async function run(files, gen) {
    await load(); gen = gen || '2005';
    const code = [];
    const pp = await mod('ivlpp', { print: s => code.push(s), printErr: () => {} });
    const args = ['-L'];
    for (const f of files) { pp.FS.writeFile('/' + f.name, f.src.endsWith('\n') ? f.src : f.src + '\n'); args.push('/' + f.name); }
    pp.callMain(args);
    const err = [];
    const c = await mod('ivl', { print: () => {}, printErr: s => err.push(s) });
    c.FS.writeFile('/ivl.conf', CONF(gen)); c.FS.writeFile('/src.v', code.join('\n') + '\n');
    try { c.callMain(['-C/ivl.conf', '--', '/src.v']); } catch (e) {}
    let vvp = null; try { vvp = c.FS.readFile('/out.vvp'); } catch (e) {}
    const eText = err.filter(l => !/system\.vpi|dynamic linking not enabled/.test(l)).join('\n');
    if (!vvp) return { ok: false, log: eText || 'compile failed', vcd: null, err: eText };
    const out = [];
    const v = await mod('vvp', { print: s => out.push(s), printErr: s => out.push(s) });

    try { v.callMain(['/sim.vvp']); } catch (e) {}
    let vcd = null; try { vcd = v.FS.readFile('/dump.vcd', { encoding: 'utf8' }); } catch (e) {}
    return { ok: true, log: out.join('\n'), vcd: vcd, err: eText };
  }
  return { run, load };
})();

    cv.width = width; cv.height = H; ctx.fillStyle = '#0a0712'; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, H);
    const end = W.end || 1, X = t => lab + (t / end) * (width - lab - 6);
    ctx.font = '11px ui-monospace,monospace'; ctx.textBaseline = 'middle';
    ctx.strokeStyle = '#2a2040'; ctx.fillStyle = '#7d72a0';
    const step = Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) * (end / 5 / Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) > 5 ? 5 : end / 5 / Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) > 2 ? 2 : 1);
    for (let t = 0; t <= end; t += step) { ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(X(t), 14); ctx.lineTo(X(t), H); ctx.stroke(); ctx.fillText(String(t), X(t) + 2, 7); }
    ids.forEach(function (id, r) {
      const v = W.vars[id], y0 = 22 + r * rowH, yh = y0 + 6, yl = y0 + rowH - 8;
      ctx.fillStyle = '#d6ccf0'; ctx.fillText(v.name.slice(0, 10), 4, y0 + rowH / 2);
      const evs = v.ev.slice(); const pts = evs.map(function (e) { return e[0]; });
      for (let k = 0; k < evs.length; k++) {
        const x1 = X(evs[k][0]), x2 = X(k + 1 < evs.length ? evs[k + 1][0] : end), val = evs[k][1];
        const bad = /[xz]/i.test(val);
        ctx.strokeStyle = bad ? '#ff7a9a' : '#7be0a4'; ctx.lineWidth = 1.5;
        if (v.w === 1) {
          const y = (val === '1') ? yh : (val === '0' ? yl : (yh + yl) / 2);
          ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1, y); ctx.lineTo(x2, y); ctx.stroke();

        }

  }
  $('#run').onclick = function () { run(); };
  $('#hint').onclick = function () { $('#hintbox').textContent = 'Hint: ' + L[cur].hint; };
