chapters.title: Behavioural modelling: always, if, case and loops

maps.title: Behavioural Verilog
links: Sensitivity list | is | always at star
Behavioural Verilog | uses | if and case
always at star | makes | Combinational logic

summary: Writing everything as assign statements gets clumsy for anything with choices. The behavioural style lets you write what the circuit does using if, case and loops inside an always block, and the tools work out the gates.

The most important lesson of the chapter is how to read an always block as hardware: a block that is sensitive to every input becomes combinational logic, and a block sensitive to a clock edge becomes flip-flops.
It also explains the difference between blocking and non-blocking assignment, the source of many beginner bugs.

glossary.def: A block of procedural code that runs again whenever something in its sensitivity list changes.
The events in @(...) that trigger the block: signal changes or clock edges.
A block sensitive to every signal it reads: combinational logic.
The = operator: executes in order, the value changes immediately.
The <= operator: right sides are read first, then all updates happen together.
An accidental latch created when a combinational block does not assign on every path.
A multi-way branch selecting on the value of an expression.

keyPoints: always @* with blocking assignments describes combinational logic; give every output a value on every path.
always @(posedge clk) with non-blocking assignments describes flip-flops.
Use if / else if for priority, case for selecting by value.
for loops in hardware are unrolled into repeated logic.
Blocking (=) is executed in order; non-blocking (<=) reads first, updates together.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Combinational building blocks: adders, multiplexers, decoders:
• Combinational circuits have no memory: outputs depend only on inputs.
• Full adder: sum = a XOR b XOR cin; cout = majority(a, b, cin).
• Subtraction: a - b = a + (not b) + 1 in two's complement.
• Mux selects, decoder one-hot decodes, priority encoder reports the highest set line.
• A ripple-carry adder's delay grows with its length because the carry must pass through every stage.

ELI5. Imagine a robot that is told: if the door is open, walk through, otherwise knock. The robot makes a decision. In hardware the decision is not made over time. Every branch exists as wires, and a switch picks the right one.

Now the real words. Inside an always block you can use if, case and loops. A block that lists every input it reads, written always @*, becomes combinational logic. A block that waits for a clock edge becomes flip-flops.

If you forget to say what an output does in some case, the circuit has to remember the old value, and you get an unwanted latch. The sign = updates now, the sign <= reads everything first and updates together.
Try it. In the lab swap two registers with = and see that both end up equal, then fix it with <=.
If you remember one thing: use = in logic, <= in clocked blocks, and always give every output a value.

Imagine a recipe that says: if the oven is hot, put the cake in, otherwise wait. That is a decision, and writing it with assign and question marks becomes hard to read when there are many cases. Verilog lets you write the decision directly with if and else, and tools turn it into gates.
But if and else may only appear inside a procedural block, and the main one is always.

An always block has a header with a sensitivity list: the events that make it run. always @(a or b or s) runs whenever any of a, b or s changes. The shorthand always @* lists every signal the block reads, automatically.
Inside, statements run in order, like a small program, and the whole block is a piece of hardware: the program is only how you describe it. (See Figure 8.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 8.1. Three always blocks and the hardware they become. A block with no clock is logic; a block on a clock edge is flip-flops; a block that forgets a branch becomes a latch.

items: Notice that y is declared output reg. Anything assigned inside an always block must be a reg. Remember what you learned: that does not mean a flip-flop. This block has no clock edge in it, so y is just a wire driven by a multiplexer. The word reg only says that the assignment is procedural.

The decisions you can write are if with else if, and case. An if chain is a priority: the first true condition wins. A case compares one expression against a list of values and is better for decoding, such as turning a number into a display pattern or choosing an ALU operation.
Always add a default branch to case, to cover every value. (See Table 8.1 below.)

lesson.title: Table 8.1. if versus case
head: if / else if
case
rows: a chain of conditions, in order

items: Here is the biggest trap in combinational blocks. If a path through the block does not assign an output, that output must remember its old value, so the tool builds a latch.

If you write if (en) q = d; with no else, q holds when en is 0, and you have a latch whether you meant it or not. The rule: in a combinational always block, assign every output on every path. A good habit is to give each output a default value on the first line. (See Table 8.2 below.)

lesson.title: Table 8.2. Combinational always: checklist
head: Check
Why
rows: so the block reacts to every input it reads
every output assigned on every path
covers values you did not list

items: Loops are allowed too. A for loop in a combinational block does not run over time. The tool unrolls it into repeated hardware. Counting the ones in a byte, for example, is a loop that adds each bit to a counter. The loop variable is an integer that exists only for the description.
Keep the number of iterations fixed so the tool can unroll it.
Now the two kinds of assignment. The blocking assignment, written =, takes effect at once, and the next line sees the new value.

The non-blocking assignment, written <=, first evaluates its right side, and schedules the update to happen at the end of the time step, after all the other right sides have been read. So all the left sides change together, like flip-flops sharing a clock edge.
(See Figure 8.2 below.) (See Table 8.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 8.2. Swapping two registers. With blocking assignment the second line reads the already-changed value; with non-blocking assignment both values are read first.

lesson.title: Table 8.3. Blocking versus non-blocking
head: Blocking  =
Non-blocking  <=
rows: at the end of the time step

items: The golden rule: use non-blocking assignments in clocked blocks and blocking assignments in combinational blocks, and never mix the two kinds in one block. Following this rule avoids a whole family of simulation races, where two blocks update each other in an unpredictable order.
(See Figure 8.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 8.3. What happens inside one simulation time step. Active events run first, then non-blocking updates land together, then anything that changed re-evaluates.

items: Behind the rule is how the simulator works. In each time step it runs all the active events, then applies the non-blocking updates, then wakes anything that changed, and repeats until nothing is left.
Because q2 <= q1 reads the old q1 in the active step, two flip-flops in a chain behave just like real ones, with q2 getting the previous value of q1.

The lab has five levels: an ALU with case, an arbiter with if and else if, a seven-segment decoder, a one-counter with a for loop, and a swap that fails with blocking assignments and works with non-blocking ones. Do the last one slowly and watch the values.
Memory trick: Equals now, arrow later. = happens Now; <= happens Later, together. 'Logic is equals, flops are arrows.'

quiz.q: What does always @* mean?
options: run whenever any signal the block reads changes
quiz.explain: It is the automatic sensitivity list.

quiz.q: How do you avoid an accidental latch?
options: assign every output on every path
quiz.explain: Missing branches mean 'remember'.

quiz.q: Which assignment should you use in a clocked always block?
quiz.explain: It models flip-flops updating together.

quiz.q: A for loop in synthesisable combinational code is...
quiz.explain: The loop count must be fixed.

quiz.q: In a case statement, what should always be included?
quiz.explain: It covers values you did not list.

Config in window.VLCFG. */
(function () {
  const CFG = window.VLCFG, L = CFG.levels, key = 'vlab:' + CFG.title;
  let done = {}, saved = {}, cur = 0, tab = 0, files = [], last = null, completed = false, busy = false;
  try { const s = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(key) || '{}'); done = s.done || {}; saved = s.code || {}; } catch (e) { }
  const $ = s => document.querySelector(s);
  const esc = s => s.replace(/[&<>]/g, c => ({ '&': '&', '<': '<', '>': '>' }[c]));
  document.body.innerHTML = '<div class="card"><h2>' + esc(CFG.title) + '</h2><div class="k" id="intro"></div></div><div class="card"><div class="chips" id="chips"></div><div id="lt"></div></div>' +
    '<div class="card"><div class="tabs" id="tabs"></div><textarea id="ed" spellcheck="false" autocapitalize="off" autocomplete="off" autocorrect="off"></textarea>' +
    '<div class="row"><button id="run">Run</button><button class="s" id="hint">Hint</button><button class="s" id="sol">Show solution</button><button class="s" id="rst">Start over</button></div>' +
    '<div id="hintbox" class="small"></div></div>' +
    '<div class="card"><b>Goals</b><ul id="goals"></ul><div id="status" class="small"></div></div>' +
    '<div class="card"><b>Console</b><pre id="con">Press Run.</pre><b>Waveform</b><div class="small" id="wnote">Signals appear after a run that dumps a VCD.</div><div class="wave" id="wave"><canvas id="cv" height="10"></canvas></div><div class="row"><button class="s" id="zin">Zoom in</button><button class="s" id="zout">Zoom out</button></div></div>';
  $('#intro').textContent = CFG.intro || '';
  let zoom = 1;
  function save() { try { localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify({ done: done, code: saved })); } catch (e) { } }
  function chips() {
    $('#chips').innerHTML = '';
    L.forEach(function (lv, i) { const b = document.createElement('button'); b.className = 'chip' + (i === cur ? ' on' : '') + (done[i] ? ' done' : ''); b.textContent = (done[i] ? '✓ ' : '') + (i + 1); b.onclick = function () { enter(i); }; $('#chips').appendChild(b); });
  }
  function tabs() {
    $('#tabs').innerHTML = '';
    files.forEach(function (f, i) { const b = document.createElement('button'); b.className = i === tab ? '' : 's'; b.textContent = f.name + (f.edit ? '' : ' (read only)'); b.onclick = function () { pull(); tab = i; push(); tabs(); }; $('#tabs').appendChild(b); });
  }
  function pull() { if (files[tab]) files[tab].src = $('#ed').value; }
  function push() { const f = files[tab]; $('#ed').value = f.src; $('#ed').readOnly = !f.edit; }
  function goalsView(res) {
    $('#goals').innerHTML = '';
    L[cur].goals.forEach(function (g, i) { const li = document.createElement('li'); const ok = res && res[i]; li.className = ok ? 'ok' : ''; li.textContent = (ok ? '✓ ' : '○ ') + g.t; $('#goals').appendChild(li); });
  }
  function enter(i) {
    cur = i; const lv = L[i];
    files = lv.files.map(function (f) { const s = saved[i + ':' + f.name]; return { name: f.name, src: (f.edit && s != null) ? s : f.src, edit: !!f.edit }; });
    tab = Math.max(0, files.findIndex(function (f) { return f.edit; }));
    $('#lt').innerHTML = '<b>' + esc(lv.title) + '</b><div class="info" style="margin-top:4px">' + lv.text.split('\n').map(function (p) { return '<p style="margin:4px 0">' + esc(p) + '</p>'; }).join('') + '</div>';
    $('#hintbox').textContent = ''; $('#con').textContent = 'Press Run.'; $('#status').textContent = ''; last = null;
    tabs(); push(); goalsView(null); chips(); drawWave(null);
  }
  function evalGoals(r) {
    return L[cur].goals.map(function (g) {
      if (g.re === 'COMPILE') return r.ok;
      return r.ok && new RegExp(g.re, 'm').test(r.log);
    });
  }
  async function run() {
    if (busy) return last; busy = true; pull();
    files.forEach(function (f) { if (f.edit) saved[cur + ':' + f.name] = f.src; });
    $('#run').disabled = true; $('#status').textContent = 'compiling and simulating…';
    let r;
    try { r = await VL.run(files.map(function (f) { return { name: f.name, src: f.src }; }), L[cur].gen); } catch (e) { r = { ok: false, log: 'engine error: ' + e, vcd: null }; }
    last = r; $('#con').innerHTML = (r.ok ? '' : '<span class="err">') + esc(r.log.replace(/^VCD info:.*\n?/m, '').replace(/^\/[\w.]+:\d+: \$finish called at.*$/m, '').trim() || '(no output)') + (r.ok ? '' : '</span>');
    const res = evalGoals(r); goalsView(res);
    const all = res.every(Boolean);
    $('#status').textContent = r.ok ? (all ? 'Level complete.' : 'Compiled. Not all goals met yet.') : 'Compile error: fix it and run again.';
    if (all) { done[cur] = 1; }
    save(); chips(); drawWave(r.vcd);
    if (!completed && L.every(function (x, i) { return done[i]; })) { completed = true; try { if (window.lilith && window.lilith.complete) window.lilith.complete(); } catch (e) { } }
    $('#run').disabled = false; busy = false; return r;
  }
  function solve(i) {
    if (i !== cur) enter(i);
    const lv = L[cur];
    files.forEach(function (f) { if (lv.solution[f.name] != null) f.src = lv.solution[f.name]; });
    push(); return run();
  }
  /* ---- waveform ---- */
  function parseVCD(t) {
    const vars = {}, order = [], scope = []; let time = 0, end = 0; const lines = t.split('\n'); let defs = true;
    for (let ln of lines) {
      ln = ln.trim(); if (!ln) continue;
      if (defs) {
        if (ln.startsWith('$scope')) scope.push(ln.split(/\s+/)[2]);
        else if (ln.startsWith('$upscope')) scope.pop();
        else if (ln.startsWith('$var')) { const p = ln.split(/\s+/); const id = p[3]; if (!vars[id]) { vars[id] = { name: p[4], w: +p[2], depth: scope.length, ev: [] }; order.push(id); } }
        else if (ln.startsWith('$enddefinitions')) defs = false;
        continue;
      }
      const c = ln[0];
      if (c === '#') { time = +ln.slice(1); if (time > end) end = time; }
      else if (c === 'b' || c === 'B') { const p = ln.split(/\s+/); if (vars[p[1]]) vars[p[1]].ev.push([time, p[0].slice(1)]); }
      else if ('01xXzZ'.indexOf(c) >= 0) { const id = ln.slice(1); if (vars[id]) vars[id].ev.push([time, c]); }
    }
    return { vars: vars, order: order, end: end };
  }
  function valAt(v, t) { let r = 'x'; for (let k = 0; k < v.ev.length; k++) { if (v.ev[k][0] <= t) r = v.ev[k][1]; else break; } return r; }
  function hex(b) { if (/[xz]/i.test(b)) return b.toLowerCase().indexOf('x') >= 0 ? 'x' : 'z'; return parseInt(b, 2).toString(16); }
  function drawWave(vcd) {
    const cv = $('#cv'); const ctx = cv.getContext('2d');
    if (!vcd) { cv.width = 10; cv.height = 10; $('#wnote').style.display = ''; return; }
    const W = parseVCD(vcd); const ids = W.order.filter(function (id) { return W.vars[id].ev.length; }).slice(0, 16);
    if (!ids.length) { cv.width = 10; cv.height = 10; return; }
    $('#wnote').style.display = 'none';
    const rowH = 30, lab = 76, base = Math.max(300, $('#wave').clientWidth || 300), width = Math.floor((base - lab) * zoom) + lab, H = ids.length * rowH + 22;
    cv.width = width; cv.height = H; ctx.fillStyle = '#0a0712'; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, H);
    const end = W.end || 1, X = t => lab + (t / end) * (width - lab - 6);
    ctx.font = '11px ui-monospace,monospace'; ctx.textBaseline = 'middle';
    ctx.strokeStyle = '#2a2040'; ctx.fillStyle = '#7d72a0';
    const step = Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) * (end / 5 / Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) > 5 ? 5 : end / 5 / Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) > 2 ? 2 : 1);
    for (let t = 0; t <= end; t += step) { ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(X(t), 14); ctx.lineTo(X(t), H); ctx.stroke(); ctx.fillText(String(t), X(t) + 2, 7); }
    ids.forEach(function (id, r) {
      const v = W.vars[id], y0 = 22 + r * rowH, yh = y0 + 6, yl = y0 + rowH - 8;
      ctx.fillStyle = '#d6ccf0'; ctx.fillText(v.name.slice(0, 10), 4, y0 + rowH / 2);
      const evs = v.ev.slice(); const pts = evs.map(function (e) { return e[0]; });
      for (let k = 0; k < evs.length; k++) {
        const x1 = X(evs[k][0]), x2 = X(k + 1 < evs.length ? evs[k + 1][0] : end), val = evs[k][1];
        const bad = /[xz]/i.test(val);
        ctx.strokeStyle = bad ? '#ff7a9a' : '#7be0a4'; ctx.lineWidth = 1.5;
        if (v.w === 1) {
          const y = (val === '1') ? yh : (val === '0' ? yl : (yh + yl) / 2);
          ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1, y); ctx.lineTo(x2, y); ctx.stroke();
          if (k > 0) { const pv = evs[k - 1][1], py = (pv === '1') ? yh : (pv === '0' ? yl : (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1, py); ctx.lineTo(x1, y); ctx.stroke(); }
        } else {
          ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1 + 2, (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.lineTo(x1 + 5, yh); ctx.lineTo(x2 - 3, yh); ctx.lineTo(x2, (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.lineTo(x2 - 3, yl); ctx.lineTo(x1 + 5, yl); ctx.closePath(); ctx.stroke();
          if (x2 - x1 > 16) { ctx.fillStyle = bad ? '#ff7a9a' : '#ffd27f'; ctx.fillText(hex(val), x1 + 8, (yh + yl) / 2); }
        }
      }
    });
  }
  $('#run').onclick = function () { run(); };
  $('#hint').onclick = function () { $('#hintbox').textContent = 'Hint: ' + L[cur].hint; };
  $('#sol').onclick = function () { const lv = L[cur]; files.forEach(function (f) { if (lv.solution[f.name] != null) f.src = lv.solution[f.name]; }); push(); $('#hintbox').textContent = 'Solution loaded. Press Run to check it, and read it line by line.'; };
  $('#rst').onclick = function () { saved = {}; Object.keys(saved).forEach(function (k) { delete saved[k]; }); enter(cur); };
  $('#zin').onclick = function () { zoom = Math.min(16, zoom * 2); if (last) drawWave(last.vcd); };
  $('#zout').onclick = function () { zoom = Math.max(1, zoom / 2); if (last) drawWave(last.vcd); };
  $('#ed').addEventListener('keydown', function (e) { if (e.key === 'Tab') { e.preventDefault(); const t = e.target, s = t.selectionStart; t.value = t.value.slice(0, s) + '  ' + t.value.slice(t.selectionEnd); t.selectionStart = t.selectionEnd = s + 2; } });
  window.__lab = { lab: CFG, enter: enter, run: run, solve: solve, isDone: function (i) { return !!done[i]; }, setCode: function (n, s) { files.forEach(function (f) { if (f.name === n) { f.src = s; } }); push(); } };
  $('#rst').onclick = function () { Object.keys(saved).forEach(function (k) { if (k.indexOf(cur + ':') === 0) delete saved[k]; }); enter(cur); };
  enter(0);
})();
</script></body></html>

chapters.title: Sequential circuits in Verilog: registers, counters and shift registers

maps.title: Sequential Verilog
links: Shift registers | convert | Serial to parallel

summary: Now we make circuits that remember. A flip-flop in Verilog is an always block with a clock edge in its sensitivity list. Add a reset, an enable and some logic in front, and you have registers, counters and shift registers.
Two decisions matter here: whether reset is synchronous or asynchronous, and how to make sure every register starts in a known state.
Almost every digital system is made from these parts, so the idioms in this chapter are ones you will write constantly.

glossary.def: A group of flip-flops holding a value.
A reset that only acts at the clock edge.
A reset that acts immediately, whatever the clock is doing.
A control that decides whether a register loads on this clock edge.
A register that adds one (or subtracts one) on each clock.
A chain of flip-flops moving bits along one place per clock.
A counter going from its maximum value back to 0.

keyPoints: A flip-flop is always @(posedge clk) q <= d;
Add reset and enable with if / else if inside the block.
Async reset adds negedge rst_n to the sensitivity list; sync reset does not.
A counter is count <= count + 1; a shift register is q <= {q[2:0], din};
Always give registers a reset so they start in a known state.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Behavioural modelling: always, if, case and loops:
• always @* with blocking assignments describes combinational logic; give every output a value on every path.
• always @(posedge clk) with non-blocking assignments describes flip-flops.
• Use if / else if for priority, case for selecting by value.
• for loops in hardware are unrolled into repeated logic.
• Blocking (=) is executed in order; non-blocking (<=) reads first, updates together.
ELI5. Imagine a row of children passing a ball. Every time the teacher claps, each child passes the ball to the next one at the same moment. Nobody passes early. The clap is the clock.

Now the real words. A flip-flop in Verilog is an always block that waits for the rising edge of the clock and then assigns with <=. Add an if for reset and one for enable. A counter adds one at every clap, and wraps around from the largest number to zero. A shift register moves bits one place along per clock. A reset puts every register in a known starting state.
Try it. In the lab build a counter, then a ring counter where a single one runs around a circle.
If you remember one thing: a clocked always block with <= is a register, and every register needs a reset.

The smallest sequential circuit is one flip-flop. In Verilog it is an always block triggered by the rising edge of the clock, assigning with the non-blocking operator: always @(posedge clk) q <= d; Everything else in this chapter is that line with more inside it.
The sensitivity list says when to act, and the body says what the next value is.

In real circuits a register must be able to hold its value, and it must start in a known state. We add an enable and a reset. With if statements it reads like English: if reset, clear; else if enable, load. The order matters: the reset is checked first and wins.
Every flip-flop in a real design should be resettable, or its first value is unknown, which the simulator shows as x.

This register uses an asynchronous reset: the sensitivity list has both the clock edge and the falling edge of the reset line, so the register clears the instant rst_n goes low. The synchronous version leaves out the reset edge and waits for the next clock edge.
Both are common. Asynchronous is quicker to react; synchronous is easier for the timing tools, because reset is just another input to the logic. (See Figure 9.1 below.) (See Table 9.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 9.1. Asynchronous reset clears q the moment rst_n falls. Synchronous reset clears it at the next rising edge.

Asynchronous

items: Counters are registers that add one. The line count <= count + 1; does it, and because the counter is four bits wide it wraps around from 15 to 0 by itself.

An up-down counter adds a direction input, and a loadable counter adds a load input with a value. The priorities are set by the order of the ifs: reset first, then load, then direction. (See Figure 9.2 below.) (See Table 9.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 9.2. A 4-bit counter: held at zero by reset, then counting up at every rising clock edge.

items: Counters are also a way to divide frequency. Bit 0 of a counter toggles every clock, so it runs at half the clock frequency. Bit 1 runs at a quarter, and so on.
A 24-bit counter on a 50 MHz clock has a top bit that blinks about three times per second, which is a classic way to make an LED blink on an FPGA board.
A shift register is a chain of flip-flops where the output of each feeds the input of the next. Every clock edge, each bit moves one place along and a new bit enters at one end.
In Verilog it is one line: q <= {q[2:0], din}; the left side takes the lower three bits and puts the new bit in the bottom. (See Figure 9.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 9.3. A 4-bit shift register. Feed in 1, 0, 1, 1 and the register reads 1011.

items: Shift registers convert between serial and parallel data. Bits arriving one at a time on a wire are collected into a word. Loaded in parallel and shifted out, they become a serial stream again.

They also make pseudo-random number generators when the incoming bit is a XOR of some of the outputs. A ring counter is a special shift register whose output feeds back to its input: a single 1 chases itself around the loop. (See Table 9.3 below.)

items: In the lab you will write a register with async reset and enable, a counter, an up-down counter with load, a shift register and a ring counter. The testbench for each uses a clock and checks the values after specific clock edges.
If your counter is off by one clock, check whether your reset is synchronous or not.
Memory trick: Reset first, enable next. Order in a register: Reset, Load, Enable, Hold: 'Real Lions Eat Humans.'

quiz.q: An asynchronous reset needs...

quiz.explain: It reacts to the reset edge itself.

quiz.q: What does a 4-bit counter do after 15?
quiz.explain: The carry out is lost.

quiz.q: In a shift register q <= {q[2:0], din}, where does din enter?

quiz.q: Why should every register have a reset?
options: so it starts in a known state
quiz.explain: Otherwise its first value is x.

    ids.forEach(function (id, r) {
      const v = W.vars[id], y0 = 22 + r * rowH, yh = y0 + 6, yl = y0 + rowH - 8;
      ctx.fillStyle = '#d6ccf0'; ctx.fillText(v.name.slice(0, 10), 4, y0 + rowH / 2);
      const evs = v.ev.slice(); const pts = evs.map(function (e) { return e[0]; });
      for (let k = 0; k < evs.length; k++) {
        const x1 = X(evs[k][0]), x2 = X(k + 1 < evs.length ? evs[k + 1][0] : end), val = evs[k][1];
        const bad = /[xz]/i.test(val);
        ctx.strokeStyle = bad ? '#ff7a9a' : '#7be0a4'; ctx.lineWidth = 1.5;
        if (v.w === 1) {
          const y = (val === '1') ? yh : (val === '0' ? yl : (yh + yl) / 2);
          ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1, y); ctx.lineTo(x2, y); ctx.stroke();
          if (k > 0) { const pv = evs[k - 1][1], py = (pv === '1') ? yh : (pv === '0' ? yl : (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1, py); ctx.lineTo(x1, y); ctx.stroke(); }
        } else {
          ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1 + 2, (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.lineTo(x1 + 5, yh); ctx.lineTo(x2 - 3, yh); ctx.lineTo(x2, (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.lineTo(x2 - 3, yl); ctx.lineTo(x1 + 5, yl); ctx.closePath(); ctx.stroke();
          if (x2 - x1 > 16) { ctx.fillStyle = bad ? '#ff7a9a' : '#ffd27f'; ctx.fillText(hex(val), x1 + 8, (yh + yl) / 2); }
        }
      }
    });
  }
  $('#run').onclick = function () { run(); };
  $('#hint').onclick = function () { $('#hintbox').textContent = 'Hint: ' + L[cur].hint; };
  $('#sol').onclick = function () { const lv = L[cur]; files.forEach(function (f) { if (lv.solution[f.name] != null) f.src = lv.solution[f.name]; }); push(); $('#hintbox').textContent = 'Solution loaded. Press Run to check it, and read it line by line.'; };
  $('#rst').onclick = function () { saved = {}; Object.keys(saved).forEach(function (k) { delete saved[k]; }); enter(cur); };
  $('#zin').onclick = function () { zoom = Math.min(16, zoom * 2); if (last) drawWave(last.vcd); };
  $('#zout').onclick = function () { zoom = Math.max(1, zoom / 2); if (last) drawWave(last.vcd); };
  $('#ed').addEventListener('keydown', function (e) { if (e.key === 'Tab') { e.preventDefault(); const t = e.target, s = t.selectionStart; t.value = t.value.slice(0, s) + '  ' + t.value.slice(t.selectionEnd); t.selectionStart = t.selectionEnd = s + 2; } });
  window.__lab = { lab: CFG, enter: enter, run: run, solve: solve, isDone: function (i) { return !!done[i]; }, setCode: function (n, s) { files.forEach(function (f) { if (f.name === n) { f.src = s; } }); push(); } };
  $('#rst').onclick = function () { Object.keys(saved).forEach(function (k) { if (k.indexOf(cur + ':') === 0) delete saved[k]; }); enter(cur); };
  enter(0);
})();

chapters.title: Time: delays, clocks, setup and hold

maps.title: Timing
links: Setup and hold | broken gives | Metastability

summary: Gates take time. A signal that changes at an input arrives at the output a little later, and a flip-flop needs its input to be stable for a moment around the clock edge. Timing decides how fast a circuit can run.

Verilog lets you write delays with a hash sign, but only for simulation: synthesis ignores them. They are for modelling and testbenches. The real timing of the chip comes from the physical gates, which static timing analysis checks.
This chapter covers the delay forms, the clock period and the setup and hold rules, plus the critical path that limits the speed of the whole chip.

glossary.def: The time between an input change and the resulting output change.
A directive that sets the time unit and the simulation precision.
A delay that swallows pulses shorter than itself, like a real gate.
How long before the clock edge data must be stable.
How long after the clock edge data must stay stable.
The slowest path between flip-flops; it sets the maximum clock frequency.
An in-between state a flip-flop may enter if its setup or hold rule is broken.

keyPoints: Delays written with # are for simulation; synthesis ignores them.
`timescale 1ns/1ps sets the unit and the resolution.
Setup and hold: data must be stable before and after the clock edge.
Clock period must cover clock-to-q, logic delay and setup time: Tclk >= tcq + tlogic + tsu.
The slowest path (critical path) sets the maximum clock frequency.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Sequential circuits in Verilog: registers, counters and shift registers:
• A flip-flop is always @(posedge clk) q <= d;
• Add reset and enable with if / else if inside the block.
• Async reset adds negedge rst_n to the sensitivity list; sync reset does not.
• A counter is count <= count + 1; a shift register is q <= {q[2:0], din};
• Always give registers a reset so they start in a known state.

ELI5. Imagine a relay race. The first runner starts at the clap, runs to the next runner, and has to arrive in time to hand over the stick before the next clap. If the runner is too slow, the baton is dropped.

Now the real words. Gates take time. Between two flip-flops, the clock period must be long enough for the first flip-flop's output to appear, for the logic to settle, and for the data to be stable a little before the next edge.

That little time before the edge is the setup time, and after it the hold time. The slowest path decides how fast the clock can run. Delays written with # are only for simulation; the real chip has its own.
Try it. In the practice section fill in the clock budget: 0.3 plus 2.2 plus 0.1.
If you remember one thing: the clock period must cover clock-to-q, logic and setup time of the slowest path.

So far every circuit answered instantly. In reality nothing is instant. When an input of a gate changes, the output follows after a propagation delay, which depends on the transistors and the wires. A chain of ten gates has ten delays.
If the chain is too slow, the answer is not ready when the next clock edge comes, and the circuit fails.

Verilog lets you model delay. In a testbench, #10 means wait ten time units. On a gate or an assign it means the output changes that long after the inputs: assign #2 y = ~a; gives an inverter with a two-unit delay.
The unit is set by the timescale directive at the top of the file, such as 1ns/1ps, which means time units are nanoseconds and simulation rounds to picoseconds. (See Table 10.1 below.)

lesson.title: Table 10.1. Delay constructs in Verilog
head: Form
Meaning
For synthesis?
rows: rise delay 1, fall delay 2 on a gate

items: There are two models of how a delay treats short pulses. An inertial delay is what real gates do: a pulse shorter than the delay does not make it through, because the output has no time to move. A transport delay just shifts everything later, pulses and all, like a long wire.
Verilog's assign delays are inertial by default. (See Figure 10.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 10.1. A two-unit pulse enters a four-unit delay. The inertial model swallows it. The transport model passes it along, shifted.

items: The most important timing facts are about flip-flops. Inside, a flip-flop samples its input at the clock edge. To do this reliably the input must be stable for a short time before the edge, the setup time, and for a short time after it, the hold time.
This forbidden window is tiny, a fraction of a nanosecond, but it is what limits the speed of the chip. (See Figure 10.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 10.2. The forbidden window around the rising clock edge. If d changes inside it, q may be wrong.

items: What happens if data changes inside the window? The flip-flop may capture the old value, the new one, or become metastable: stuck for a while near the middle voltage, neither 0 nor 1.

Metastability resolves itself eventually, but the output may be late and wrong. It cannot be removed, only made very unlikely, for example by passing signals from another clock through two flip-flops in a row. (See Table 10.2 below.)

lesson.title: Table 10.2. Timing parameters
head: Symbol
Name
Meaning
Typical size
rows: delay from clock edge to the new q
delay through the gates between two flip-flops
data stable this long before the edge
data stable this long after the edge

items: Now put the pieces together. Consider two flip-flops with some logic between them. At a clock edge the first one launches new data. It appears at its output after tcq, travels through the logic in tlogic, and must reach the second flip-flop at least tsu before the next edge.
So the clock period must be at least the sum of all three. The slowest such path in the chip is the critical path, and it decides the maximum clock frequency. (See Figure 10.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 10.3. The clock period must cover the clock-to-q delay, the logic delay and the setup time of the capturing flip-flop.

items: A worked example. If tcq is 0.3 ns, the logic takes 2.2 ns and tsu is 0.1 ns, the period must be at least 2.6 ns. That is about 385 MHz.
To go faster, shorten the critical path: use a faster adder, split the logic over two clock cycles by inserting a register (pipelining), or reduce the load on the slow nets. (See Table 10.3 below.)

lesson.title: Table 10.3. Ways to meet a tight clock
head: Technique
How it helps
Price
rows: splits long logic by adding registers
latency grows by one cycle per stage

items: Hold violations are the opposite problem. If data from the launching flip-flop reaches the capturing one too fast, it changes inside the hold window of the same edge.

Slowing the clock does not fix a hold problem, since both sides scale. Tools fix it by inserting delay buffers. For RTL beginners the rule is simple: use one clock, register your outputs, and let the tools check timing.

In the next chapter's lab, one level adds a two-unit delay to an inverter and asks you to read the shifted times from the printout. It is the only delay you will model by hand in this course. After that we turn to the practical art of testing designs.
Memory trick: Tcq plus logic plus setup. Clock period covers tcq + logic + setup: 'Clock, Logic, Setup: C-L-S.'

chapters.title: Testbenches: how to know your design works

maps.title: Testbenches
links: Test | must be able to | Fail

summary: A design you have not tested is a design that does not work. A testbench is a Verilog module with no ports that creates a clock, applies inputs, watches the outputs and says pass or fail.
You will learn the structure of a testbench, the system tasks that print and record, how to loop over all inputs, how to use random numbers against a reference, and why a test must be able to fail.
Good habits here are worth more than any other skill in this course: professional chip teams spend more time on verification than on design.

glossary.def: A module that wraps the design under test (DUT) and supplies its stimulus.
Design under test.
The input values and clocks a testbench applies.
A testbench that compares outputs to expected values and prints pass or fail by itself.
A simple, obviously correct description of what the DUT should compute.
A recording of signals over time that a viewer can display.
A reusable block of testbench code, called like a procedure.

keyPoints: A testbench has no ports: reg for inputs, wire for outputs, an instance of the DUT, and an initial block.
Generate a clock with always #5 clk = ~clk;
Use display and monitor tasks to print, dumpfile and dumpvars to record a waveform, finish to stop.
Self-checking tests compare to a reference and count errors.
A test that cannot fail proves nothing: include corner cases and boundaries.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Time: delays, clocks, setup and hold:
• Delays written with # are for simulation; synthesis ignores them.
• `timescale 1ns/1ps sets the unit and the resolution.
• Setup and hold: data must be stable before and after the clock edge.
• Clock period must cover clock-to-q, logic delay and setup time: Tclk >= tcq + tlogic + tsu.
• The slowest path (critical path) sets the maximum clock frequency.

ELI5. Imagine you built a toy car and want to know if it works. You would put it on a test track, push the start button, and watch. A good test track has steep hills and sharp corners, because easy tests do not find the problems.

Now the real words. A testbench is a Verilog module with no ports. It contains the design under test, makes a clock, applies inputs, and compares the outputs to the right answers, then prints pass or fail.
Loops can try every input. Random numbers can try many. The most important rule is that a test must be able to fail: include equal values, zero and the biggest values, where the bugs hide.
Try it. In the lab a comparator has a bug and the testbench says it is fine. Add the one test that exposes it.
If you remember one thing: a test that cannot fail proves nothing, so test the boundaries.

Imagine you have built a coffee machine. You would not hand it to customers without pressing buttons and tasting the result. A testbench is that for a circuit. It is a module with no ports, because it is the whole world around the design.
Inside it you place the design under test, give it a clock, drive its inputs, and look at what comes out. (See Figure 11.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 11.1. A self-checking testbench. A stimulus generator drives the design and a reference model; a checker compares and reports.

items: Read the structure. Inputs are regs because the testbench drives them from procedural code. Outputs are wires because the DUT drives them. The DUT is instantiated by name.

The initial block runs once: it starts the waveform recording, sets inputs, waits with the hash delay, prints, and ends. Without a finish task a clock-driven simulation would run forever. (See Table 11.1 below.)

lesson.title: Table 11.1. Testbench system tasks
head: Task
Does
Example use
rows: show a value at one moment
print every time any listed signal changes
record every signal into a waveform file

items: Sequential designs need a clock. A clock is a signal that flips every half period. The standard recipe is two lines: reg clk = 0; always #5 clk = ~clk;. The always block with only a delay repeats forever, inverting clk every 5 time units, so the period is 10 units.
With a timescale of 1 ns that is a 100 MHz clock. (See Figure 11.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 11.2. A clock generated with always #5 clk = ~clk. Rising edges occur at 5, 15 and 25.

items: How many inputs should you test? For a full adder there are only 3 input bits: eight cases. Test them all with a loop. A for loop in a testbench is real code that runs over time: put the loop counter on the inputs, wait a moment, and compare the outputs to what Verilog's own plus operator gives.
This is exhaustive testing, and it is the best kind when it is affordable.

Notice the !== operator. It compares exactly, including x and z, and gives a plain 0 or 1. If the DUT's output were x, an ordinary comparison would give x, and the if would quietly treat it as false, hiding the error. Use the case equality operators in testbenches.
The expression a + b + cin on the right is the reference model: a simple trusted calculation of the answer.

When the inputs are too many to try all of them, use random tests. dollar-random gives a random number each time. Apply a few hundred or thousand random input pairs, check each against the reference, and count the failures.
Random testing finds surprising bugs, but add a few directed tests too: zero, the maximum value and, above all, boundaries. (See Table 11.2 below.)

lesson.title: Table 11.2. Testing strategies
head: Strategy
How
Best when
rows: you pick interesting cases by hand
compare automatically, print pass or fail
always; do not rely on staring at waveforms

items: A test that cannot fail proves nothing. Imagine a comparator that wrongly says a is greater than b when they are equal. A test that only tries a = 1, b = 2 and a = 3, b = 1 passes. Only a = b exposes the bug.

This is why testers always try boundaries: equal values, zero, maximum, wrap-around. The third lab level hands you a buggy design and a weak testbench, and asks you to add the vectors that make it fail. (See Table 11.3 below.)

lesson.title: Table 11.3. Typical testbench mistakes
head: Mistake
Effect
Remedy
rows: always end with the finish task
comparing with == when x is possible
reading outputs at the same instant as inputs change
wait a few time units first

items: Finally, look at the waveform. Self-checking tests tell you whether something is wrong. The waveform tells you why. Zoom in around the failure and trace backwards through the signals.

The labs include a small waveform viewer under the console for exactly this reason. A good habit: when a test fails, read the first failure, not the last, since later ones are often consequences of it.

The lab for this chapter turns the tables: the circuit is given and you write the testbench. You build a clock, an exhaustive loop, a bug-catching test and a random test, and then give an inverter a delay to see its effect on the waveform.
Memory trick: A test must be able to fail. Boundaries break things: Equal, Zero, Max, Wrap. 'Every Zebra Must Wander.'

quiz.q: Why does a testbench have no ports?
options: It is the outermost module that surrounds the design
Ports are not allowed in simulation
quiz.explain: It generates inputs and watches outputs itself.

quiz.q: How do you make a clock with a period of 10?
quiz.explain: Toggle every half period.

quiz.q: Why use !== instead of != in a check?
options: so that x and z are caught as mismatches
quiz.explain: It never returns x.

quiz.q: What makes a testbench self-checking?
options: it compares outputs to expected values and reports pass or fail
quiz.explain: No human needs to inspect it.

quiz.q: Which input values find boundary bugs best?
quiz.explain: Bugs often hide at the edges.

always #5 clk = ~clk;
if (out !== expected) errors
a test must be able to fail

    const ds = new DecompressionStream('deflate-raw');

    return new Uint8Array(await new Response(ds.readable).arrayBuffer());
  }

    ready = (async () => {

        const s = document.createElement('script'); s.textContent = js; document.head.appendChild(s);

  /* files: [{name, src}]; returns {ok, log, vcd, err} */
  async function run(files, gen) {
    await load(); gen = gen || '2005';
    const code = [];
    const pp = await mod('ivlpp', { print: s => code.push(s), printErr: () => {} });
    const args = ['-L'];
    for (const f of files) { pp.FS.writeFile('/' + f.name, f.src.endsWith('\n') ? f.src : f.src + '\n'); args.push('/' + f.name); }
    pp.callMain(args);
    const err = [];
    const c = await mod('ivl', { print: () => {}, printErr: s => err.push(s) });
    c.FS.writeFile('/ivl.conf', CONF(gen)); c.FS.writeFile('/src.v', code.join('\n') + '\n');
    try { c.callMain(['-C/ivl.conf', '--', '/src.v']); } catch (e) {}
    let vvp = null; try { vvp = c.FS.readFile('/out.vvp'); } catch (e) {}
    const eText = err.filter(l => !/system\.vpi|dynamic linking not enabled/.test(l)).join('\n');

    return { ok: true, log: out.join('\n'), vcd: vcd, err: eText };
  }
  return { run, load };

  }

  function parseVCD(t) {
    const vars = {}, order = [], scope = []; let time = 0, end = 0; const lines = t.split('\n'); let defs = true;
    for (let ln of lines) {
      ln = ln.trim(); if (!ln) continue;
      if (defs) {
        if (ln.startsWith('$scope')) scope.push(ln.split(/\s+/)[2]);
        else if (ln.startsWith('$upscope')) scope.pop();
        else if (ln.startsWith('$var')) { const p = ln.split(/\s+/); const id = p[3]; if (!vars[id]) { vars[id] = { name: p[4], w: +p[2], depth: scope.length, ev: [] }; order.push(id); } }
        else if (ln.startsWith('$enddefinitions')) defs = false;

      }

    }
    return { vars: vars, order: order, end: end };
  }
  function valAt(v, t) { let r = 'x'; for (let k = 0; k < v.ev.length; k++) { if (v.ev[k][0] <= t) r = v.ev[k][1]; else break; } return r; }
  function hex(b) { if (/[xz]/i.test(b)) return b.toLowerCase().indexOf('x') >= 0 ? 'x' : 'z'; return parseInt(b, 2).toString(16); }
  function drawWave(vcd) {
    const cv = $('#cv'); const ctx = cv.getContext('2d');
    if (!vcd) { cv.width = 10; cv.height = 10; $('#wnote').style.display = ''; return; }
    const W = parseVCD(vcd); const ids = W.order.filter(function (id) { return W.vars[id].ev.length; }).slice(0, 16);
    if (!ids.length) { cv.width = 10; cv.height = 10; return; }
    $('#wnote').style.display = 'none';
    const rowH = 30, lab = 76, base = Math.max(300, $('#wave').clientWidth || 300), width = Math.floor((base - lab) * zoom) + lab, H = ids.length * rowH + 22;
    cv.width = width; cv.height = H; ctx.fillStyle = '#0a0712'; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, H);
    const end = W.end || 1, X = t => lab + (t / end) * (width - lab - 6);
    ctx.font = '11px ui-monospace,monospace'; ctx.textBaseline = 'middle';
    ctx.strokeStyle = '#2a2040'; ctx.fillStyle = '#7d72a0';
    const step = Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) * (end / 5 / Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) > 5 ? 5 : end / 5 / Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) > 2 ? 2 : 1);
    for (let t = 0; t <= end; t += step) { ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(X(t), 14); ctx.lineTo(X(t), H); ctx.stroke(); ctx.fillText(String(t), X(t) + 2, 7); }
    ids.forEach(function (id, r) {
      const v = W.vars[id], y0 = 22 + r * rowH, yh = y0 + 6, yl = y0 + rowH - 8;
      ctx.fillStyle = '#d6ccf0'; ctx.fillText(v.name.slice(0, 10), 4, y0 + rowH / 2);
      const evs = v.ev.slice(); const pts = evs.map(function (e) { return e[0]; });
      for (let k = 0; k < evs.length; k++) {
        const x1 = X(evs[k][0]), x2 = X(k + 1 < evs.length ? evs[k + 1][0] : end), val = evs[k][1];
        const bad = /[xz]/i.test(val);

          const y = (val === '1') ? yh : (val === '0' ? yl : (yh + yl) / 2);
          ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1, y); ctx.lineTo(x2, y); ctx.stroke();
          if (k > 0) { const pv = evs[k - 1][1], py = (pv === '1') ? yh : (pv === '0' ? yl : (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1, py); ctx.lineTo(x1, y); ctx.stroke(); }
        } else {
          ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1 + 2, (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.lineTo(x1 + 5, yh); ctx.lineTo(x2 - 3, yh); ctx.lineTo(x2, (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.lineTo(x2 - 3, yl); ctx.lineTo(x1 + 5, yl); ctx.closePath(); ctx.stroke();
          if (x2 - x1 > 16) { ctx.fillStyle = bad ? '#ff7a9a' : '#ffd27f'; ctx.fillText(hex(val), x1 + 8, (yh + yl) / 2); }
        }
      }
    });
  }
  $('#run').onclick = function () { run(); };
  $('#hint').onclick = function () { $('#hintbox').textContent = 'Hint: ' + L[cur].hint; };
  $('#sol').onclick = function () { const lv = L[cur]; files.forEach(function (f) { if (lv.solution[f.name] != null) f.src = lv.solution[f.name]; }); push(); $('#hintbox').textContent = 'Solution loaded. Press Run to check it, and read it line by line.'; };
  $('#rst').onclick = function () { saved = {}; Object.keys(saved).forEach(function (k) { delete saved[k]; }); enter(cur); };

  $('#rst').onclick = function () { Object.keys(saved).forEach(function (k) { if (k.indexOf(cur + ':') === 0) delete saved[k]; }); enter(cur); };
  enter(0);
})();

chapters.title: Finite state machines: designing circuits that follow a plan

maps.title: State machines
links: Mealy | output from | State and input

summary: A finite state machine, or FSM, is a circuit that is always in one of a small number of states, and moves between them depending on its inputs. Traffic lights, vending machines, protocol controllers and sequence detectors are all FSMs.
Every FSM has the same three parts: a state register, next-state logic and output logic. The Moore style makes outputs depend only on the state; the Mealy style also uses the inputs.
This chapter gives a method: draw the diagram, choose state names, then write the three parts in Verilog.

glossary.def: A situation the machine can be in, remembered by flip-flops.
A move from one state to another, taken at a clock edge depending on inputs.
Outputs depend only on the current state.
Outputs depend on the current state and the current inputs.
How states are written in bits: binary, one-hot, and so on.
A constant local to a module, used to name states.
The combinational logic that decides which state comes next.

keyPoints: An FSM has a state register, next-state logic and output logic.
Moore: output = f(state). Mealy: output = f(state, input).
Name the states with localparam and use a case on the state.
Write the state register in a clocked always block with <=, and the next-state and output logic in combinational blocks.
Always reset the FSM to a known initial state.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Testbenches: how to know your design works:
• A testbench has no ports: reg for inputs, wire for outputs, an instance of the DUT, and an initial block.
• Generate a clock with always #5 clk = ~clk;
• Use display and monitor tasks to print, dumpfile and dumpvars to record a waveform, finish to stop.
• Self-checking tests compare to a reference and count errors.
• A test that cannot fail proves nothing: include corner cases and boundaries.

ELI5. Imagine a vending machine. It does not remember everything that ever happened. It only remembers a small amount: how much money is in it. That amount is its state. Each coin moves it to a new state, and when it reaches the price it gives out a drink.

Now the real words. A finite state machine is always in one of a few states, remembered by flip-flops. Next-state logic decides where to go on each clock, and output logic decides what to show. In a Moore machine the output depends only on the state. In a Mealy machine it also depends on the input. You draw circles and arrows first, then write the three parts in Verilog.
Try it. In the lab finish the machine that detects the bits 1, 0, 1 in a stream, even when two patterns overlap.
If you remember one thing: draw the states and arrows first, then the Verilog follows.

Think of a turnstile at a station. It has two situations: locked and unlocked. Drop a coin while it is locked and it unlocks. Push while it is unlocked and it locks again. These situations are called states. The coin and the push are inputs.
The rule that says what state comes next is the transition. That is a complete state machine, drawn on the back of a napkin.

Any FSM, however big, is made of three pieces. A register of flip-flops remembers the current state. Next-state logic looks at the current state and the inputs and decides which state comes next. Output logic decides what the outputs are.
The register is clocked, the other two are combinational, and the state loops back to the next-state logic. (See Figure 12.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 12.1. The three parts of every FSM. The dashed arrow is the extra path that makes a machine a Mealy machine.

items: There are two flavours of output. In a Moore machine, outputs depend only on the state: a traffic light shows red because it is in the red state.

In a Mealy machine, outputs may also depend on the inputs right now, so they can react a clock cycle earlier and often need fewer states. Mealy outputs can also change when an input changes between clock edges, which makes them more sensitive to glitches. (See Table 12.1 below.)

Here is the recipe. First, list the states and name them. Second, draw the diagram: a circle for each state, an arrow for each transition, labelled with the input that causes it (and the output, for Mealy). Third, check every state has an arrow for every possible input.
Fourth, write the Verilog: names with localparam, state register, next-state case, outputs.

The first example is a traffic light with three states in a loop: red, then green, then yellow, then red again. The outputs are simply which light is on. Because the outputs depend only on the state, it is a Moore machine.
In Verilog the next-state logic is a case statement, and each output is an assign comparing the state with a name. (See Figure 12.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 12.2. A Moore traffic light. The outputs are decoded from the state.

items: Look at the three parts in the code. The first block is the state register: a clocked block with a synchronous reset that goes to a known state. The second is a combinational block, with a case on the state; every branch assigns next, and the default branch covers unused codes.
The last three lines are the output logic.

The second example is a sequence detector: it watches a stream of bits, one per clock, and raises an output when it has just seen the pattern 1, 0, 1. It needs to remember how much of the pattern it has matched so far.
S0 means nothing matched, S1 means a 1 has been seen, S2 means 1 and 0 have been seen. A 1 in S2 completes the pattern. (See Figure 12.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 12.3. A Mealy detector for 101. Arc labels are input over output. The detection arc goes to S1 because the final 1 might begin another 101.

items: Why does the detection arc go back to S1 and not S0? Because the last 1 of one 101 can be the first 1 of the next: in the stream 10101 the pattern appears twice, overlapping. Getting such cases right is the main skill in FSM design.
Always ask: after the last input, what is the longest useful partial match I still have? (See Table 12.2 below.) (See Table 12.3 below.)

lesson.title: Table 12.3. Pitfalls

Cure
rows: forgetting to assign next in a branch
give next a default at the top: next = state;
reset to a named initial state
outputs from a Mealy block glitching

items: The vending machine in the lab shows how the same method scales. It remembers the credit in three states: nothing, five, ten. Coins arrive as a five or a ten. When the credit reaches fifteen, a dispense signal goes high and the machine returns to the start.
All the thinking is in the diagram; the Verilog then follows it line by line.

In the lab you complete four machines: a toggle button, the traffic light, the 101 detector and the vending machine. For each one the state register is given or easy, and your job is the next-state logic and the outputs. Draw the diagram on paper first. It really helps.
Memory trick: State, next, output. Every FSM: State register, Next-state logic, Output logic: 'SNO': Snow. Moore = State only, Mealy = Mixed with input.

quiz.q: What does a Moore machine's output depend on?
quiz.explain: A traffic light shows its state.

quiz.q: Which three parts does every FSM have?
options: state register, next-state logic, output logic
quiz.explain: Register, then two combinational blocks.

quiz.q: Why name states with localparam?
options: to make the code readable and safe
quiz.explain: Names beat bare numbers.

quiz.q: In the 101 detector, why does the detecting arc go to S1?
options: the last 1 may start the next 101
quiz.explain: Overlapping patterns.

quiz.q: Which encoding uses one flip-flop per state?
quiz.explain: Only one bit is high.

    '<div class="card"><div class="tabs" id="tabs"></div><textarea id="ed" spellcheck="false" autocapitalize="off" autocomplete="off" autocorrect="off"></textarea>' +
    '<div class="row"><button id="run">Run</button><button class="s" id="hint">Hint</button><button class="s" id="sol">Show solution</button><button class="s" id="rst">Start over</button></div>' +
    '<div id="hintbox" class="small"></div></div>' +
    '<div class="card"><b>Goals</b><ul id="goals"></ul><div id="status" class="small"></div></div>' +
    '<div class="card"><b>Console</b><pre id="con">Press Run.</pre><b>Waveform</b><div class="small" id="wnote">Signals appear after a run that dumps a VCD.</div><div class="wave" id="wave"><canvas id="cv" height="10"></canvas></div><div class="row"><button class="s" id="zin">Zoom in</button><button class="s" id="zout">Zoom out</button></div></div>';
  $('#intro').textContent = CFG.intro || '';
  let zoom = 1;
  function save() { try { localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify({ done: done, code: saved })); } catch (e) { } }
  function chips() {
    $('#chips').innerHTML = '';
    L.forEach(function (lv, i) { const b = document.createElement('button'); b.className = 'chip' + (i === cur ? ' on' : '') + (done[i] ? ' done' : ''); b.textContent = (done[i] ? '✓ ' : '') + (i + 1); b.onclick = function () { enter(i); }; $('#chips').appendChild(b); });
  }
  function tabs() {
    $('#tabs').innerHTML = '';
    files.forEach(function (f, i) { const b = document.createElement('button'); b.className = i === tab ? '' : 's'; b.textContent = f.name + (f.edit ? '' : ' (read only)'); b.onclick = function () { pull(); tab = i; push(); tabs(); }; $('#tabs').appendChild(b); });
  }
  function pull() { if (files[tab]) files[tab].src = $('#ed').value; }
  function push() { const f = files[tab]; $('#ed').value = f.src; $('#ed').readOnly = !f.edit; }
  function goalsView(res) {
    $('#goals').innerHTML = '';
    L[cur].goals.forEach(function (g, i) { const li = document.createElement('li'); const ok = res && res[i]; li.className = ok ? 'ok' : ''; li.textContent = (ok ? '✓ ' : '○ ') + g.t; $('#goals').appendChild(li); });
  }
  function enter(i) {
    cur = i; const lv = L[i];
    files = lv.files.map(function (f) { const s = saved[i + ':' + f.name]; return { name: f.name, src: (f.edit && s != null) ? s : f.src, edit: !!f.edit }; });
    tab = Math.max(0, files.findIndex(function (f) { return f.edit; }));
    $('#lt').innerHTML = '<b>' + esc(lv.title) + '</b><div class="info" style="margin-top:4px">' + lv.text.split('\n').map(function (p) { return '<p style="margin:4px 0">' + esc(p) + '</p>'; }).join('') + '</div>';
    $('#hintbox').textContent = ''; $('#con').textContent = 'Press Run.'; $('#status').textContent = ''; last = null;
    tabs(); push(); goalsView(null); chips(); drawWave(null);
  }
  function evalGoals(r) {
    return L[cur].goals.map(function (g) {
      if (g.re === 'COMPILE') return r.ok;
      return r.ok && new RegExp(g.re, 'm').test(r.log);
    });
  }
  async function run() {
    if (busy) return last; busy = true; pull();
    files.forEach(function (f) { if (f.edit) saved[cur + ':' + f.name] = f.src; });
    $('#run').disabled = true; $('#status').textContent = 'compiling and simulating…';
    let r;
    try { r = await VL.run(files.map(function (f) { return { name: f.name, src: f.src }; }), L[cur].gen); } catch (e) { r = { ok: false, log: 'engine error: ' + e, vcd: null }; }
    last = r; $('#con').innerHTML = (r.ok ? '' : '<span class="err">') + esc(r.log.replace(/^VCD info:.*\n?/m, '').replace(/^\/[\w.]+:\d+: \$finish called at.*$/m, '').trim() || '(no output)') + (r.ok ? '' : '</span>');
    const res = evalGoals(r); goalsView(res);
    const all = res.every(Boolean);
    $('#status').textContent = r.ok ? (all ? 'Level complete.' : 'Compiled. Not all goals met yet.') : 'Compile error: fix it and run again.';
    if (all) { done[cur] = 1; }
    save(); chips(); drawWave(r.vcd);
    if (!completed && L.every(function (x, i) { return done[i]; })) { completed = true; try { if (window.lilith && window.lilith.complete) window.lilith.complete(); } catch (e) { } }
    $('#run').disabled = false; busy = false; return r;
  }
  function solve(i) {
    if (i !== cur) enter(i);
    const lv = L[cur];
    files.forEach(function (f) { if (lv.solution[f.name] != null) f.src = lv.solution[f.name]; });
    push(); return run();
  }
  /* ---- waveform ---- */
  function parseVCD(t) {
    const vars = {}, order = [], scope = []; let time = 0, end = 0; const lines = t.split('\n'); let defs = true;
    for (let ln of lines) {
      ln = ln.trim(); if (!ln) continue;
      if (defs) {
        if (ln.startsWith('$scope')) scope.push(ln.split(/\s+/)[2]);
        else if (ln.startsWith('$upscope')) scope.pop();
        else if (ln.startsWith('$var')) { const p = ln.split(/\s+/); const id = p[3]; if (!vars[id]) { vars[id] = { name: p[4], w: +p[2], depth: scope.length, ev: [] }; order.push(id); } }
        else if (ln.startsWith('$enddefinitions')) defs = false;
        continue;
      }
      const c = ln[0];
      if (c === '#') { time = +ln.slice(1); if (time > end) end = time; }
      else if (c === 'b' || c === 'B') { const p = ln.split(/\s+/); if (vars[p[1]]) vars[p[1]].ev.push([time, p[0].slice(1)]); }
      else if ('01xXzZ'.indexOf(c) >= 0) { const id = ln.slice(1); if (vars[id]) vars[id].ev.push([time, c]); }
    }
    return { vars: vars, order: order, end: end };
  }
  function valAt(v, t) { let r = 'x'; for (let k = 0; k < v.ev.length; k++) { if (v.ev[k][0] <= t) r = v.ev[k][1]; else break; } return r; }
  function hex(b) { if (/[xz]/i.test(b)) return b.toLowerCase().indexOf('x') >= 0 ? 'x' : 'z'; return parseInt(b, 2).toString(16); }
  function drawWave(vcd) {
    const cv = $('#cv'); const ctx = cv.getContext('2d');
    if (!vcd) { cv.width = 10; cv.height = 10; $('#wnote').style.display = ''; return; }
    const W = parseVCD(vcd); const ids = W.order.filter(function (id) { return W.vars[id].ev.length; }).slice(0, 16);
    if (!ids.length) { cv.width = 10; cv.height = 10; return; }
    $('#wnote').style.display = 'none';
    const rowH = 30, lab = 76, base = Math.max(300, $('#wave').clientWidth || 300), width = Math.floor((base - lab) * zoom) + lab, H = ids.length * rowH + 22;
    cv.width = width; cv.height = H; ctx.fillStyle = '#0a0712'; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, H);
    const end = W.end || 1, X = t => lab + (t / end) * (width - lab - 6);
    ctx.font = '11px ui-monospace,monospace'; ctx.textBaseline = 'middle';
    ctx.strokeStyle = '#2a2040'; ctx.fillStyle = '#7d72a0';
    const step = Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) * (end / 5 / Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) > 5 ? 5 : end / 5 / Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log10(end / 5 || 1))) > 2 ? 2 : 1);
    for (let t = 0; t <= end; t += step) { ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(X(t), 14); ctx.lineTo(X(t), H); ctx.stroke(); ctx.fillText(String(t), X(t) + 2, 7); }
    ids.forEach(function (id, r) {
      const v = W.vars[id], y0 = 22 + r * rowH, yh = y0 + 6, yl = y0 + rowH - 8;
      ctx.fillStyle = '#d6ccf0'; ctx.fillText(v.name.slice(0, 10), 4, y0 + rowH / 2);
      const evs = v.ev.slice(); const pts = evs.map(function (e) { return e[0]; });
      for (let k = 0; k < evs.length; k++) {
        const x1 = X(evs[k][0]), x2 = X(k + 1 < evs.length ? evs[k + 1][0] : end), val = evs[k][1];
        const bad = /[xz]/i.test(val);
        ctx.strokeStyle = bad ? '#ff7a9a' : '#7be0a4'; ctx.lineWidth = 1.5;
        if (v.w === 1) {
          const y = (val === '1') ? yh : (val === '0' ? yl : (yh + yl) / 2);
          ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1, y); ctx.lineTo(x2, y); ctx.stroke();
          if (k > 0) { const pv = evs[k - 1][1], py = (pv === '1') ? yh : (pv === '0' ? yl : (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1, py); ctx.lineTo(x1, y); ctx.stroke(); }
        } else {
          ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x1 + 2, (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.lineTo(x1 + 5, yh); ctx.lineTo(x2 - 3, yh); ctx.lineTo(x2, (yh + yl) / 2); ctx.lineTo(x2 - 3, yl); ctx.lineTo(x1 + 5, yl); ctx.closePath(); ctx.stroke();
          if (x2 - x1 > 16) { ctx.fillStyle = bad ? '#ff7a9a' : '#ffd27f'; ctx.fillText(hex(val), x1 + 8, (yh + yl) / 2); }
        }
      }
    });
  }
  $('#run').onclick = function () { run(); };
  $('#hint').onclick = function () { $('#hintbox').textContent = 'Hint: ' + L[cur].hint; };
  $('#sol').onclick = function () { const lv = L[cur]; files.forEach(function (f) { if (lv.solution[f.name] != null) f.src = lv.solution[f.name]; }); push(); $('#hintbox').textContent = 'Solution loaded. Press Run to check it, and read it line by line.'; };
  $('#rst').onclick = function () { saved = {}; Object.keys(saved).forEach(function (k) { delete saved[k]; }); enter(cur); };
  $('#zin').onclick = function () { zoom = Math.min(16, zoom * 2); if (last) drawWave(last.vcd); };
  $('#zout').onclick = function () { zoom = Math.max(1, zoom / 2); if (last) drawWave(last.vcd); };
  $('#ed').addEventListener('keydown', function (e) { if (e.key === 'Tab') { e.preventDefault(); const t = e.target, s = t.selectionStart; t.value = t.value.slice(0, s) + '  ' + t.value.slice(t.selectionEnd); t.selectionStart = t.selectionEnd = s + 2; } });
  window.__lab = { lab: CFG, enter: enter, run: run, solve: solve, isDone: function (i) { return !!done[i]; }, setCode: function (n, s) { files.forEach(function (f) { if (f.name === n) { f.src = s; } }); push(); } };
  $('#rst').onclick = function () { Object.keys(saved).forEach(function (k) { if (k.indexOf(cur + ':') === 0) delete saved[k]; }); enter(cur); };
  enter(0);
})();
</script></body></html>

chapters.title: Building big: hierarchy, parameters, generate, functions and memories
summary: A real design has hundreds of modules, many of them variations of the same thing. Verilog has tools for reuse: parameters to change widths, generate loops to repeat structures, functions to share calculations, and arrays for memories.
This chapter shows how to turn a fixed 8-bit register into a register of any width, build an N-bit adder from a loop, write a function, and describe a ROM and a RAM.
These tools let you write a design once and use it many times.

glossary.def: A constant of a module that can be overridden when the module is instantiated.
Compile-time repetition of hardware using a genvar loop.
A loop variable that exists only at compile time, for generate loops.
A reusable combinational calculation that returns one value.
A reusable block of procedural code; mostly used in testbenches.
An array of registers: reg [7:0] mem [0:15] is 16 words of 8 bits.
Text macros and file inclusion handled before compilation.

keyPoints: module m #(parameter N = 8)(...) makes the width a knob; instantiate with m #(.N(12)).
generate for (genvar) repeats hardware at compile time.
A function returns a value computed from its inputs, with no delays.
A memory is an array: reg [7:0] mem [0:15]; read it with mem[addr].
Write once, reuse many times: that is the aim of every feature here.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Finite state machines: designing circuits that follow a plan:
• An FSM has a state register, next-state logic and output logic.
• Moore: output = f(state). Mealy: output = f(state, input).
• Name the states with localparam and use a case on the state.
• Write the state register in a clocked always block with <=, and the next-state and output logic in combinational blocks.
• Always reset the FSM to a known initial state.
ELI5. Imagine a cookie cutter. With one cutter you can make a hundred cookies, all the same. Now imagine you could turn a knob on the cutter and make the cookies bigger or smaller.

Now the real words. A parameter is that knob: the same module can be made 3 bits wide or 12 bits wide. A generate loop places many copies of the same hardware, like a long adder. A function is a calculation you can reuse. A memory is an array of registers: you give it an address and it gives back a word, and a RAM also lets you write.
Try it. In the lab turn a fixed 8-bit register into one of any width with a single parameter.
If you remember one thing: write a module once, then reuse it with parameters, generate, functions and arrays.
Suppose you wrote an 8-bit register last week, and today you need a 12-bit one and a 3-bit one. Copying and editing the file three times is a recipe for bugs. Verilog's answer is parameters.
A parameter is a constant declared in the module header, with a default value, that the instantiating module can override. (See Figure 13.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 13.1. One parameterised module used twice, at widths 12 and 3.

items: The widths in the port list are written in terms of N. When an instance says #(.N(12)), the whole module is created with N equal to 12. If the instance says nothing, the default of 8 applies. This is how libraries of adders, FIFOs and counters are written: one source, any size.
(See Table 13.1 below.)

lesson.title: Table 13.1. Parameters and friends
head: Item
Meaning
Changeable?
rows: module constant that cannot be overridden
text replacement macro, global to the file

items: Sometimes a parameter changes not just a width but the amount of hardware. An N-bit ripple adder has N full adders. You could write them by hand, but with a generate loop you write one and ask for N copies.
The loop runs while the design is being built, not while it runs: a genvar is a compile-time counter, and each iteration places another instance of the hardware.

Each iteration of the generate loop creates a block named fa, with an instance inside it, so the copies are called fa[0].f, fa[1].f and so on. The carry wires c[i] and c[i+1] join each copy to its neighbour. Change N to 32 and you get a 32-bit ripple adder, with no other change.
Next, functions. A function computes a value from its inputs and returns it: no delays, no clocks. It is ideal for a calculation used in several places, such as converting binary to Gray code.

Inside the function you assign the result to the function's own name. A function can be called anywhere an expression is allowed. Tasks are similar but may contain delays and several outputs, and are mostly used in testbenches. (See Table 13.2 below.)
Now memories. A memory in Verilog is just an array of registers. The declaration reg [7:0] mem [0:15]; makes 16 words of 8 bits each. You index it with an address: mem[5] is one word.

A ROM, a read-only memory, is filled once, often in an initial block, and read with an assign. A RAM can also be written: on a clock edge, if the write enable is high, the addressed word takes the input data. (See Figure 13.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 13.2. A 16 by 8 memory. The address selects one word; a clocked write happens when we is 1.

items: This RAM has a clocked write and an immediate, combinational read. Real FPGA block memories often have a clocked read, and the tools are happy with either as long as you follow their coding style.
Synthesis maps arrays like this to the dedicated memory blocks in an FPGA, or to a memory generator in an ASIC, so you do not build them from individual flip-flops. (See Table 13.3 below.)

Two last conveniences. The define macro replaces a name by text everywhere it is used, for example a fixed bus width. The include directive pastes another file in at that point, which is handy for shared constants.
Both are handled before the compiler sees the code, by the preprocessor, and they are the first stage in the toolchain you will run in the labs.

In the lab you build a register of any width, an N-bit adder with a generate loop, a Gray-code function, a ROM of squares and a RAM. The ROM level uses an initial block with a for loop to fill the array; that is the simplest way to create contents without an external file.
Memory trick: Knob, loop, array. Reuse: parameter is a Knob, generate is a Loop, memory is an Array.

quiz.q: How do you override a parameter N when instantiating a module?
quiz.explain: Use the #(...) list.

quiz.q: What is a genvar?
options: a loop counter used at compile time in generate loops
quiz.explain: It only exists while the design is built.

quiz.q: What does reg [7:0] mem [0:15]; declare?
quiz.explain: Word width goes before the name, depth after.

quiz.q: A function in Verilog...
options: returns one value, with no delays
quiz.explain: It is a combinational calculation.

quiz.q: Which keyword cannot be overridden at instantiation?
quiz.explain: localparam is fixed inside the module.

/* Verilog engine: Icarus Verilog (ivlpp, ivl, vvp) in WebAssembly, from VeriSim (GPL-2.0). Offline. */
window.__VLM = {};
const VL = (function () {
  const B = window.VL_BLOBS;
  async function inflate(b64) {
    const bin = atob(b64), u = new Uint8Array(bin.length);
    for (let i = 0; i < bin.length; i++) u[i] = bin.charCodeAt(i);
    const ds = new DecompressionStream('deflate-raw');
    const w = ds.writable.getWriter(); w.write(u); w.close();
    return new Uint8Array(await new Response(ds.readable).arrayBuffer());
  }
  const wasm = {}; let ready = null;
  function load() {
    if (ready) return ready;
    ready = (async () => {
      for (const n of ['ivlpp', 'ivl', 'vvp']) {
        const js = new TextDecoder().decode(await inflate(B[n + '_js']));
        wasm[n] = await inflate(B[n + '_wasm']);
        const s = document.createElement('script'); s.textContent = js; document.head.appendChild(s);
      }
    })();
    return ready;
  }
  const mod = (n, o) => window.__VLM[n](Object.assign({ wasmBinary: wasm[n] }, o));
  const CONF = g => 'basedir:/\nmodule:system.vpi\ngeneration:' + g + '\ngeneration:no-specify\nout:/out.vvp\niwidth:32\nwidthcap:65536\nfunctor:cprop\nfunctor:nodangle\nflag:DLL=vvp.tgt\n';
  /* files: [{name, src}]; returns {ok, log, vcd, err} */
  async function run(files, gen) {
    await load(); gen = gen || '2005';
    const code = [];
    const pp = await mod('ivlpp', { print: s => code.push(s), printErr: () => {} });
    const args = ['-L'];
    for (const f of files) { pp.FS.writeFile('/' + f.name, f.src.endsWith('\n') ? f.src : f.src + '\n'); args.push('/' + f.name); }
    pp.callMain(args);
    const err = [];
    const c = await mod('ivl', { print: () => {}, printErr: s => err.push(s) });
    c.FS.writeFile('/ivl.conf', CONF(gen)); c.FS.writeFile('/src.v', code.join('\n') + '\n');
    try { c.callMain(['-C/ivl.conf', '--', '/src.v']); } catch (e) {}
    let vvp = null; try { vvp = c.FS.readFile('/out.vvp'); } catch (e) {}
    const eText = err.filter(l => !/system\.vpi|dynamic linking not enabled/.test(l)).join('\n');
    if (!vvp) return { ok: false, log: eText || 'compile failed', vcd: null, err: eText };
    const out = [];
    const v = await mod('vvp', { print: s => out.push(s), printErr: s => out.push(s) });

$dumpvars(0, tb);\n    errs = 0;\n    addr = 4'd0; #5;\n    if (dout !== 8'd0) begin errs = errs + 1; $display(\"FAIL: addr=%0d -> dout=%0d, expected 0\", addr, dout); end\n    addr = 4'd1; #5;\n    if (dout !== 8'd1) begin errs = errs + 1;
